rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 render at full size and again at 4x on the base and the crown. The FAIL stands, and the core of the claim is correct, but two details in it need correcting before anyone fixes against it.

MEASURED GEOMETRY (pixel bbox of all non-background plant pixels): x 140-295, y 110-317, i.e. 156 px wide x 208 px tall = w/h 0.75. The packet demands aspect 2.5 (a creeping mat two and a half times wider than tall). The render is 3.3x wrong in the wrong direction: it is taller than wide. Notably 0.75 is almost exactly the Blueberry row's aspect 0.8 from the same batch page -- this is the family's generic upright twiggy-shrub chassis emitted verbatim for a species whose whole identity is that it is NOT that.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a solid brown woody mass rises from the baseline, narrow (~12 px) at the soil and FLARING upward like an inverted wedge, then splitting into roughly six brown canes that arc outward into a vase. Along the canes sit lance/oval leaves ~18 px long in a greyed sage-green, alternate on both sides. Five terminal rosettes of red berries -- 6-7 round berries each, packed touching, with white specular dots -- cap the cane tips.

MUST-READS, ONE BY ONE:
1. 'a wiry creeping mat over bog moss' -- ABSENT. No mat, no moss, no bog. Rows 309-317 (the bottom 9 px of the plant) contain only 10-14 plant pixels total, i.e. the trunk and nothing else. Nothing spreads horizontally at ground level anywhere in the image.
2. 'tiny leaves along hair-thin runners' -- ABSENT. The stems are thick opaque brown canes ~6-8 px wide, not hair-thin, and they are vertical, not trailing. The trunk is a single perfectly straight vertical capsule running from a rounded stub at the bottom up into the fog, roughly x=196..246, i.e. UNIFORM WIDTH with zero taper and zero crook. FOLIAGE -- the claim 'soft amorphous green fog blob' is HALF WRONG and this matters, because the foliage primitive is already built and only needs redeploying. There are roughly 25 distinct drawn leaf sprigs radiating around the crown RIM. At 3x each one is clearly a rachis bearing many tiny paired leaflets in two ranks, and they do read as fine feathery pinnate foliage -- mustRead 1 is essentially satisfied where the sprigs actually appear. The real defect is placement, not absence: every sprig sits on the outer rim pointing outward, and the entire crown INTERIOR is undifferentiated gaussian green fog with no leaf structure at all, so the mass reads as vapour with a fringe. Fix = scatter the existing sprig primitive through the crown volume and drop the fog opacity, not 'draw foliage'.

THE TWO DARK LENSES -- the claim 'unexplained dark lens shapes ... reading as a render artifact' and 'no straw-coloured seed pods anywhere' is WRONG. At 8x both shapes are unmistakably SEED PODS: elongated, gently curved, with a chain of round bead-like seed swellings visible along the inside of the outline -- textbook legume pod geometry. One sits at approx (215,130) tilted about 20deg, the other at approx (150,190) buried in the left sprig cluster and nearly invisible. So the pod geometry EXISTS and is correct in form. What fails is (a) colour -- they are dark olive/near-black instead of pale straw, so they read as holes punched in the canopy rather than fruit; (b) count -- two, where the row asks for 'bunches'; (c) attachment -- they float flat inside the fog with no peduncle and no hanging orientation, one of them horizontal-ish rather than pendant. Recolour to pale straw, multiply into hanging clusters, and attach them to something, and this must-read is met.

THORNS -- the claim is CORRECT. No thorns anywhere on the silhouette edge; nothing protrudes from the trunk or any sprig. The nearest candidates are 8-9 pale cream horizontal dashes painted on the trunk face (several stacked as pairs, e.g. two at y~265, two at y~325-340), which may be an attempted thorn or lenticel pass, but they lie entirely flat INSIDE the trunk silhouette with no protrusion and read as bark scars or birch-style ticks. mustRead 2 ('paired straight thorns at the nodes') is absent -- and it cannot be satisfied until nodes exist, i.e. until the tree gets branches.

NET: 1 of 3 must-reads readable (feathery pinnate foliage, rim only), 1 absent (thorns), 1 absent on every term (crooked low-branching dark trunk + wide flat crown). Every cane carries fern-like fronds: a rachis with roughly 18-22 tiny linear pinnules per frond, each pinnule a pale sage dab over a dark green shadow. The clusters are deep crimson/carmine (peak 176,32,64-ish with grey-lilac 152,152,168 speculars), not pink; and the recolour is not confined to the tips -- the foliage palette WAS changed too. Raspberry's dominant greens quantise to 128,160,104 / 136,168,112 / 120,144,96 (pale grey-sage); Blackberry's to 16,40,16 / 56,112,40 / 64,120,40 (saturated dark green). Three of the five clusters -- clearest on the top-right one -- show a distinct dark void at the centre of the drupelet ring, and that void is precisely what distinguishes them from Blackberry, whose identical clusters have a solid tan/orange RECEPTACLE PLUG filling the same spot (botanically the correct differentiator, receptacle pulls free on raspberry and stays in on blackberry). The artist did attempt the hollow core and it half-lands. The genuine fruit defect is the one the judge got right in the other half of the sentence: there is no thimble. No individual berry exists at all -- the drupelets are laid out as a flat annular wreath of 8 spheres facing the viewer, so the head reads as a pincushion flower / allium umbel, not as a domed conical aggregate fruit. The centre-top head is a solid striated dome with no ring and no hole, so it does not carry the read either.

DEFECTS THE JUDGE MISSED.
(a) LEAF FORM IS THE WRONG ORGAN, and this is the primary failure. The spec is 'pinnate leaves of 3-5 toothed leaflets'. At 16x each frond is unmistakably a fern/bipinnate lace of ~20 tiny undifferentiated linear pinnules. There is not one broad ovate toothed leaflet anywhere in the image. Combined with the wreath heads the whole plant reads as a mimosa/acacia or a red-flowered yarrow, not a bramble.

CORRECTION 1 -- the seed spike is NOT '2px'. It is a column of about eight stacked round beads, 9px wide at its widest and 36px tall (y89-y124), sitting bolt upright on a bare 25px length of rachis above the topmost leaf pair. Colour #8b2645-#9b2a4b, a decent crimson. So it is genuinely present and it is genuinely crimson -- but it is a rigidly ERECT bead skewer, not a plume, and it carries zero droop, zero mass and zero fringe. At 36px it is 14.5% of plant height; the amaranth tassel should be the visual centre of gravity, a heavy drooping fleshy mass that outweighs the foliage. MUST-READ 1 ('thick fleshy plume or drooping tassel of seed') is therefore FAILED, but for the right reason: not 'too small to see' -- it is visible -- it is the wrong SHAPE and the wrong WEIGHT. The fix is a broad, multi-branched, arching/nodding panicle several times this width, not merely a taller version of the same bead thread.

CORRECTION 2 -- 'barely taller than one leaflet' is misleading. The spike (36px) is TWICE the depth of a leaflet (18px) but well short of a leaflet's 48px length. Sizing the fix against 'one leaflet' will underbuild it; size it against the 98px width and 178px height of the leaf mass.

CORRECTION 3 -- the claim never names the worst colour defect. MUST-READ 2 is 'strong crimson stem and veins'. The stem is #463219, a flat dark olive-brown for its entire length including the exposed 34px of bare stalk below the foliage -- no crimson anywhere on it. Meanwhile the LEAVES are a uniform dusty rose-pink (#b15460 core, #73353f shading) with no green at all, when the packet's leafColour is 'mid green, frequently flushed crimson'. The palette is inverted: the crimson that belongs on the stem and veins was poured over the whole blade, and the green that belongs on the blade is gone. That inversion is what makes the frond read as decorative-pink rather than as a crop. Veining does exist -- there are fine darker midrib and lateral lines inside each blade -- but they are the same pink family as the blade, so they do not deliver 'crimson veins'.

MUST-READ 3 ('big soft broad leaves') FAILED, and worse than stated: the packet also specifies ALTERNATE arrangement on a THICK GROOVED stem, and what is drawn is strictly OPPOSITE on a smooth uniform-width twig. So the leaf spec is wrong on shape (lance, not broad oval-diamond), on phyllotaxy (opposite, not alternate), and on stem character (smooth thin rachis, not thick grooved stalk). The identical 16px pitch across all eleven pairs is itself a defect -- real amaranth foliage is irregular and the lower leaves are much larger.

BAND: FAIL stands. Zero of the three must-reads survive, and the composite silhouette names a different organism (fern/compound frond). This is not a polish-level miss.

rows.readsAs: an ornamental gold grass with a brass screw pushed into it
rows.defect: The single feature that makes barley unmistakable — awns longer than the head itself, fanning up in a long bristling sweep — is reduced to a small flared cap sitting on top of a short ribbed cylinder, so the awns are shorter than the ear rather than several times longer. The head is also ramrod upright when the must-read demands it nod over when ripe. The head object is identical to the one on Millet, Oats, Rice, Rye and Sorghum.
rows.fix: Draw the awns as a long fanned sweep two to three times the ear's length streaming up and back, and tip the whole ear over on a bent neck.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld after looking at the 440x440 PNG at 1x and at 6x/10x crops of the ear (source box approx x180-240, y85-175). The FAIL claim is accurate on every point; two details need correcting because they understate the defect, and four further defects the judge did not name should go into the fix.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A wide fountain-shaped fan of about 16 narrow, smoothly tapering, arching blades rising from a single point on the ground shadow, plus ONE dead-vertical thread-thin culm through the centre carrying a single ear at roughly y=85-175. Everything - blades, culm, ear - is the same straw-gold. The read is ornamental fountain grass / pampas / a gold dracaena fan, with a brass countersunk screw standing in the middle of it.

CORRECTION 1 - the awns are not 'a small flared cap', they are not awns at all. At 10x the structure above the ear is a SOLID FILLED trapezoid/funnel: one continuous gold shape, hard straight edges, flat top, no internal strands, no gaps, no taper to points. There is not a single individual awn filament anywhere in the image. The judge described it as a flared cap that is too short, which reads as 'the awns exist but need lengthening'; in fact the awn geometry has to be built from scratch as a fan of discrete near-parallel bristles. Measured: cap approx 15 px tall over an ear approx 42 px tall, so approx 0.35x, against a mustRead of longer than the head itself (barley runs 1.0-1.5x). It is a 3-4x miss, not a trim.

CORRECTION 2 - the 'screw' read has a second cause the judge did not name: the ear OUTLINE. The ear is a straight-sided rectangle of constant width with a hard flat cut-off base and a hard flat top, and inside it run exactly two perfectly regular parallel columns of identical small chevron/scale marks with a dark seam down the middle. Constant width + machine-regular chevrons = thread. A barley ear is a tapered spike whose outline is BUMPY because each plump spikelet bulges past the axis; nothing here bulges. mustRead 3 ('grains in tight rows') is therefore only half-credited: rows are present, grain is not - the marks read as milled thread, not as plump kernels.

CONFIRMED - 'ramrod upright instead of nodding' is exactly right. The culm and ear are plumb vertical with zero curvature over their whole length; the tip of the ear sits directly above the base of the culm. mustRead 2 (head nods over when ripe) is absent outright.

FURTHER DEFECTS NOT IN THE ORIGINAL CLAIM. (a) The leaf spec is 'broad flat blades clasping a jointed hollow culm' - the blades drawn are narrow whip/needle blades at maybe a quarter of the width they need, and none of them clasp or even touch the culm; the culm is a bare separate thread passing through the fan. (b) No nodes/joints and no leaf sheaths anywhere on the culm - it is a featureless line. (c) leafColour is 'mid green, ripening straw gold' and the asset is 100% gold with no green at any point, which is a large part of why it reads ornamental rather than as a food crop. (d) Proportion: the leaf fan is roughly 3x the height and 8x the visual mass of the ear, and there is only one culm - barley should show several culms whose ears carry the silhouette above a modest basal tuft. Here the ear is a small ornament on a big grass clump.

BAND. Of three mustReads, the defining one (extremely long fanned awns, longer than the head) is absent as a form, the nod is absent, and the grain rows read as screw thread. The asset does not read as barley; it reads as an ornamental grass with a countersunk screw in it. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a green caterpillar or a fern frond
rows.defect: Same leaf-ladder column as Amaranth, Potato and Quinoa with only the leaflet outline changed. The leaflets are plain rounded ovals — the arrowhead/heart shape that is the first must-read is nowhere on the asset. The stem is plain green, not red-flushed or jointed, and the three-angled pyramid seeds are absent; the only harvest cue is one small white blob at the apex.
rows.fix: Rebuild as a sparse open broadleaf herb with a handful of large alternate arrowhead leaves on a red jointed stem, and hang visible sharply three-sided brown seeds under the flower clusters.
rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, with corrections and additions. WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CANVAS (440x440, plant bbox roughly x174-300, y100-325): a single straight vertical olive stem carrying about ten tightly stacked OPPOSITE leaf pairs. The pairs overlap so densely that the left and right leaf tips form a continuous scalloped/segmented outer edge, and the whole plant reads as one solid vertical block - a green caterpillar or a bird feather / pinnate fern frond, not a broadleaf herb. Above the topmost leaf pair, on a short bare stem, sits one small flat white crescent cap (approx x200-240, y100-118) - the only non-green element on the asset. A soft elliptical ground shadow sits at the base; the stem runs bare from y~300 to the shadow.

MUST-READ 1, arrowhead leaves - GENUINELY ABSENT. Judge is correct and their description is accurate. Every leaf is a broad obovate/rounded blade: widest at mid-length, blunt ROUNDED apex, tapering smoothly into the stem with NO basal lobes, NO sagittate/hastate flare, no pointed tip. Each has a simple pinnate herringbone midrib+side-vein pattern. Nothing anywhere on the asset carries an arrowhead or heart silhouette. This is the first-read identity feature and it is missing.

MUST-READ 2, red-flushed jointed stem - GENUINELY ABSENT. Verified by pixel sampling, not eyeballing: lower stem at (220,300..320) = R62 G84 B27; mid stem at (220,200..250) = R129 G150 B83. R is BELOW G at every sample - pure olive/yellow-green, zero red or magenta anywhere in the stem. There are also no swollen nodes or joint bands drawn; the stem is one unbroken smooth taper. Judge correct.

MUST-READ 3, sharply three-angled pyramid seeds - GENUINELY ABSENT. No seed, achene, triangle, pyramid or brown element exists anywhere on the asset. Judge correct.

CORRECTIONS / ADDITIONS THE JUDGE MISSED (these matter for the fix):
(a) The judge said the harvest is simply absent. Half of it is actually attempted: the white crescent at the crown is the flower cluster. But it renders as a single flat white mushroom-cap / lollipop arc perched on a bare stalk - it does not read as 'loose clusters of small white-pink flowers'. It needs to become several airy sprays of tiny white-pink florets on branching pedicels, and it needs to be pink-tinged, not chalk white. Do not delete it; rebuild it.
(b) The leaves are OPPOSITE (perfectly mirrored pairs at each node). The packet specifies ALTERNATE. This is a second, unmentioned spec violation and it is exactly what creates the caterpillar/frond read - the mirrored pairs plus the dense node spacing produce the segmented ladder silhouette. Fixing leaf shape alone will not fix the read; the phyllotaxy must go alternate and the internodes must open up so individual leaves separate against the background.
(c) Silhouette proportion is wrong. Packet aspect is 0.80; the leaf mass measures roughly 115px wide by 210px tall, about 0.50-0.55. It is far too narrow and columnar for a bushy broadleaf herb.
(d) Leaf count/density: ~20 leaves crammed into ~200px of stem with near-zero visible gap. A buckwheat herb should read as a sparse open plant, few large leaves on long petioles, with background visible between them. There are no petioles at all here - blades attach directly to the stem.

VERDICT: three of three must-reads fail, and the organism reads as the wrong kingdom-level thing (an insect larva or a fern frond, not a flowering broadleaf crop). FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a young hemp or cannabis bush
rows.defect: The palmate narrow-fingered leaflets on red-brown canes do carry the right leaf idea, but the leaflets are drawn at a fraction of the size the reference calls for (large palmate leaves), so they read as small hemp leaves scattered along bare sticks. The petioles are not distinguishable in colour from the canes, so the striking red leaf-stalk cue is lost, and the cluster of fat tapering tubers at the base — the entire reason cassava is a staple crop — is absent; the stems just vanish into the shadow.
rows.fix: Enlarge the palmate leaves three-fold on visible red petioles and draw four or five fat tapering brown tubers radiating out from the stem base.

rows.readsAs: a bamboo cane with a pink palm flower and a pine cone stuck to it
rows.defect: None of the three must-reads survives. The top tassel is a stiff radiating pink-salmon fan that reads as an anemone or palm inflorescence, not a feathery straw-coloured tassel. The cob is a bare brown pointed cone with a spray of stiff yellow spokes fanning off its tip — it reads as a shuttlecock or a cone with a broom, with no green husk and no soft drooping silk. The stalk is a slim jointed bamboo pole carrying only five narrow leaves, not a thick solid stalk with wide arching strap leaves, and there is no white midrib.
rows.fix: Sheathe the cob in green husks with soft drooping pale silk at its tip, recolour the top tassel to feathery straw, and thicken the stalk with wide white-midribbed strap leaves in two alternating ranks.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at full size and at 5x crops of the crown, the cob node, a single leaf and the bare stalk. The FAIL stands, but three of the stated causes are factually wrong and must not be fixed as written.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. Stalk: a perfectly straight, constant-width dark-olive vertical pole running the full 440px height, crossed by five or six pale sage horizontal node bands that overhang the stalk edge by a few pixels on the left. Constant width plus protruding node collars is exactly the bamboo read the first judge described, and it is correct: a corn culm should be thicker, should taper toward the top, and its nodes should be hidden under wrapping leaf sheaths rather than drawn as free-floating dashes. No leaf sheath clasps the stem anywhere on this asset.

CORRECTION 1 - leaf count. There are SIX leaves, not five: right at y~125, left at y~170, right at y~220 (partly behind the cob), left at y~260, right at y~305, left at y~350 of 440. They strictly alternate side to side, so mustRead #3's 'alternating ranks' is genuinely SATISFIED and should not be listed as a defect.

CORRECTION 2 - the leaves are NOT midrib-less. Each blade carries a pale sage highlight stripe running its full length. The real defect is subtler: the stripe is set close to the upper edge of the blade rather than down the centre, so it reads as a rim-light on the leaf's top curve rather than as a rib, and it is sage-green where the packet asks for a WHITE midrib on a BRIGHT green blade. The blades are also thin for corn (roughly 8:1 length-to-width) where the packet wants 'very long BROAD strap leaves', and they are muted olive rather than bright green. Fix the midrib's position, whiteness and the blade width - do not add a midrib that already exists.

CORRECTION 3 - there IS a green husk, just a token one. At the base of the cob sits a rounded, spade-shaped pale-green bract overlapping the cob's lower-left quadrant and butting against the stem at a node. It covers roughly the bottom quarter of the cob and reads as a small stray leaf, not a sheath. So 'no green husk' is wrong as stated; the accurate defect is that the husk does not SHEATHE - about three quarters of the cob is bare and the bract does not wrap around it.

WHAT GENUINELY FAILS. (a) The crown is a radially symmetric fan of about twelve smooth, equal-length, salmon-pink tapered rays springing from a solid pink triangular cup, spread over roughly 160 degrees. It is stiff, symmetric, and pink - it reads as a palm frond, a gerbera, or a feather duster. mustRead #1 asks for a FEATHERY tassel: a loose, asymmetric, drooping branched panicle in straw/tan/green with fine pendent anthers. Nothing about hue, structure or softness matches; only the position at the very top is right. (b) The cob body is a chocolate-brown pointed ellipse carrying only faint darker vertical striations - no kernel grid, no yellow, no green husk over it. It reads as a pine cone or a protea bud. (c) The silk is a fan of about ten straight, stiff, evenly spaced golden ROD-like spokes radiating from the cob tip over roughly 120 degrees, all the same length. mustRead #2 asks for a soft SILK TUFT: fine, limp, unequal, drooping threads. Rigid radial spokes are the opposite.

NET. The topology of all three must-reads is present - crown flower at the apex, fruiting body at mid-height on the side of the stem at a leaf joint, alternating strap leaves - and cob-on-the-side-at-a-node is a genuinely corn-specific placement that partly rescues the asset. But the colour signalling is wrong in every load-bearing place (salmon-pink where straw is required, chocolate-brown where green-husk-plus-gold-kernel is required, muted olive where bright green is required), and both the tassel and the silk are drawn as the same stiff radial spoke-fan primitive, which is what makes the plant read as an ornamental bamboo carrying a palm flower and a cone. Two of three must-reads fail in character. FAIL is upheld.

PRIORITISED FIXES: 1) replace the pink radial fan with a straw/pale-tan branched drooping panicle - several unequal side branches, each hung with fine spikelets, asymmetric. 2) Wrap the cob in overlapping green husk leaves that taper past its tip, leaving only a small window of pale-gold kernel rows, and replace the gold spoke fan with a soft drooping tuft of unequal fine silk threads emerging from the husk tip. 3) Thicken and taper the culm, suppress the protruding node dashes, and let each leaf base wrap the stem as a sheath. 4) Centre and whiten the existing leaf midribs, widen the blades, and shift the leaf green brighter.

rows.readsAs: a yellow-green ornamental grass clump with a small ear
rows.defect: The straight central cane with a single dense grain head over arching narrow blades is roughly the right idea, but the head is a thin short cylinder — nothing like the thick bottlebrush the must-read asks for — and it carries the same flared trapezoid cap the other five grasses wear, which adds an awn-like flare millet does not have. It is the identical fountain silhouette used for Barley, Oats, Rice, Rye and Sorghum with only a hue change.
rows.fix: Fatten the head into a plump cylindrical bottlebrush three times its current width, packed with visible round beads, and delete the flared cap.

rows.readsAs: a cream grass clump with a screw head on a stick
rows.defect: The reference states the identity as a negative: no compact ear and no bristling awn mass, just a loose spreading panicle of teardrop spikelets dangling on fine threads. What is drawn is exactly the forbidden thing — a compact ribbed ear with a bristling flared cap, the same head object as Barley and Rye. The delicate open silhouette is replaced by the same dense fountain of blades. The asset directly contradicts its own must-read.
rows.fix: Replace the ear entirely with an airy branched panicle of dangling teardrop spikelets on thin drooping threads, and thin the leaf clump so light shows through.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verified at 8x zoom on the head crop (source px x195-255, y90-200) and at 3x on the whole plant. The FAIL stands, and the core of the claim is correct, but two details in it need correcting.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. One perfectly straight vertical olive-gold culm rises from the centre of a dense radial fountain of roughly 28-32 cream-gold strap blades that all spring from a single narrow ground point and arch outward, the outermost pairs sweeping almost horizontal to the left and right edges of the canvas. At the top of the culm sits a COMPACT RIBBED EAR: a narrow vertical spike about 90px tall and 26px wide, built as two ranks of short blocky grain segments stacked in a tight ladder either side of a black central rachis line that is visible down the middle. There is no gap, no branch, no pedicel anywhere in it - it is one solid two-rank ear, exactly the compact ear the mustRead forbids. Capping it is a splayed crown of about ten short straight bristles fanning upward and outward into a trapezoid - an awn mass, also explicitly forbidden.

MUST-READS, ONE BY ONE. (1) 'loose spreading panicle with grains hanging on fine threads' - ABSENT. Zero branching. Nothing hangs. There is not a single teardrop spikelet, not a single fine thread, no pendulous element anywhere in the image. (2) 'no compact ear and no bristling awn mass' - BOTH VIOLATED, as described above. (3) 'delicate open silhouette' - ABSENT. The silhouette is a heavy solid fan; the blades overlap into an unbroken opaque wedge for the lower two thirds, and the seed head is the densest solid mass in the frame.

CORRECTIONS TO THE OTHER JUDGE'S WORDING. (a) 'Identical to Barley's' is overstated. I rendered Barley.png at the same crop for comparison. The two are the SAME CHASSIS - same straight culm, same two-rank ribbed ear with a black rachis, same top flare, same radial blade fountain - but they are not pixel-identical: Barley's ear sits off-centre to the left and is shorter and fatter, its awn cap is a SOLID filled trapezoidal wedge, whereas Oats' ear is centred, longer and narrower, and its cap is a COMB of individually separated bristles. So the correct statement is 'the same forbidden ear archetype as Barley, differing only in ear proportion and in whether the awn flare is solid or combed' - not 'identical'. (b) 'the same dense fountain' is fair and correct; Oats' fountain is if anything denser and wider-spreading than Barley's, with more blades and a lower outermost sweep.

OTHER NOTES FOR THE FIX. Aspect reads roughly correct (wide, ~0.35 by the leaf spread). Colour is off-brief in a minor way: the reference asks for 'light green, ripening cream-gold' and the asset is uniformly cream-gold with only the culm carrying any olive - acceptable as a ripened state, and not part of the failure. The failure is entirely structural: this asset reads as a second barley/wheat, not as oats. The fix is to delete the ribbed ear and the awn crown outright and replace them with a branched panicle - a central axis whose top third throws off 4-6 tiers of thin whorled branches, each branch ending in one or two teardrop spikelets hanging point-down on a hair-thin pedicel, with clear dark background visible THROUGH the head. The blade fountain should also be thinned so the silhouette reads open.

rows.readsAs: a fern, or a bottlebrush conifer sprig
rows.defect: Leaf-ladder chassis again, here with dozens of tiny identical feathery leaflets stacked in two dense ranks — the opposite of the specified pinnate leaf of LARGE terminal leaflets with small leaflets between them, so the uneven-sized leaflet cue that makes a potato leaf recognisable is gone. There is one lone white star flower instead of a cluster, and no yellow anther cone. Most damaging: no tubers and no stolons at the base at all, so a plant grown entirely for its tubers shows none.
rows.fix: Draw a few large terminal leaflets with small ones interleaved on a sprawling angular stem, and add a knot of knobbly brown eyed tubers on short stolons at the base.
rows.verifyWhy:
I looked at the full 440x440 render and then at 5-11x magnified crops of the base, the flower and a single side-branch, plus a pixel histogram of the whole canvas. The FAIL stands, and the core of the claim is correct, but several details need correcting so the fix targets the right things.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A single rigidly vertical pale-green stem, ~4px wide, runs the full height. Off it spring roughly nine PAIRS of thin dark-green side-rachises, angled up-and-out at a constant angle, perfectly mirrored left/right. Each rachis carries a dense row of about fourteen small pale oval-to-comma leaflets. Total leaflet count is north of 200. The ink bounding box is x175-267 by y102-324, i.e. 93px wide by 223px tall. It reads as a fern frond or a mimosa/Acacia shoot stood on end.

MUST-READ 1 — 'compound leaf of uneven-sized leaflets': ABSENT. The judge said 'dozens of tiny identical feathery leaflets'; at 11x there IS a mild size gradient, the leaflets nearest the main stem are noticeably fatter and hook-shaped and they taper toward each rachis tip. So 'identical' is slightly overstated. But that gradient is a fern-pinna taper, not the potato signature, which is a SHORT rachis carrying only about 3-4 PAIRS of large ovate terminal-sized leaflets with tiny interstitial leaflets tucked in the gaps between them. The render has the wrong count by two orders of magnitude and the wrong size relationship. Also correct the judge on 'conifer': the leaflets are rounded ovals, not needles, so 'fern frond' is the accurate read and 'conifer sprig' is not.

MUST-READ 2 — 'clusters of white or purple star flowers with a yellow cone of anthers': FAILS HARDER than claimed. There is exactly one flower, at the very apex, and the judge is right that it has no anther cone: the histogram finds only 23 yellow pixels in the entire image (antialias fringe) and the magnified centre of the bloom is flat pure white with no disc, cone or dot of any kind. Two things the judge missed. First, the flower is SOLITARY and terminal, so the 'clusters' half of the must-read fails too, not just the anther cone. Second, it has SEVEN narrow free-standing petals splayed as a star; the potato corolla is five fused petals forming a shallow pentagonal rim, so even the petal geometry is wrong, not merely the missing centre.

MUST-READ 3 — 'knobbly tubers hanging on stolons at the base': ABSENT, exactly as claimed, and I confirmed it two ways. The magnified base crop shows the bare 4px stem descending unbranched into a plain elliptical ground shadow, with no stolons, no root mass and nothing below the soil line. The whole-image histogram finds ONE orange/brown pixel in 9,310 ink pixels; 8,913 are green and ~230 are the white flower. There is no tuber anywhere on the canvas. For the one species in this family that is grown solely for its tuber, this alone is disqualifying.

TWO FURTHER DEFECTS THE JUDGE DID NOT NAME, worth fixing in the same pass. (a) ASPECT. The packet specifies aspect 1 and 'sprawling angular stems'; the render is a 93x223 spire, an effective aspect near 0.42, and it is bilaterally symmetric to the pixel, which is the opposite of sprawling and angular. (b) COLOUR. The packet asks for 'dull mid-green, matt and slightly rough'; the leaflets are rendered a bright, high-key yellow-green with a soft glow, which pushes it further toward ornamental-fern territory.

All three must-reads fail. The asset does not read as a potato; it reads as a fern.  FAIL upheld.

rows.readsAs: a pale bottlebrush or a fuzzy caterpillar on a pin
rows.defect: The mealy pale-green toothed leaves are the right colour and roughly the right outline, but they are packed onto the same rectangular leaf-ladder column as Amaranth, Buckwheat and Potato, which quinoa never looks like — quinoa is an open leafy herb topped by a chunky branched panicle. That panicle, the must-read that carries the identity and the hot cream/magenta/orange colour, is drawn as a single thin red bead thread poking out of the top. The grooved striped stem is a bare hairline.
rows.fix: Shrink the leaf mass and crown the plant with a broad chunky branched seed panicle in magenta-orange at least as wide as the foliage.
rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG at full size and then at 4x-8x nearest-neighbour crops of the head, the leaf column and the base. The FAIL stands, and the original judge's description is substantially accurate, but two points need correcting and one missed defect needs adding.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A single strictly vertical column of pale sage/khaki-cream foliage, ~150px wide by ~230px tall, occupying the middle of the frame with parallel vertical left and right edges. The foliage is built from SEVEN identical mirrored whorl rows stacked one on top of the other on an invisible central axis; each row is a fan of 5-6 narrow lanceolate blades per side, each row is the same width as the one above it, and each node is marked by a dark radial shading seam at the centreline. The top row closes off into a symmetric star/rosette. The result is a rectangular ladder column - a bottlebrush or a small conifer spike - not an open leafy herb. The original judge's 'shared rectangular ladder column' and 'pale bottlebrush caterpillar' read are both correct.

MUST-READ 1, DUCK-FOOT (GOOSEFOOT) LEAF - ABSENT. This is the largest failure and the judge underweighted it. At 4x every blade is a plain narrow pointed lanceolate leaflet with a SMOOTH ENTIRE MARGIN and a single central crease. There is not one lobe, not one tooth, not one broad triangular blade anywhere in the ~80 leaflets drawn. The packet asks for 'goosefoot-shaped, broad and irregularly toothed, alternate' - what is drawn is narrow, untoothed, and strictly opposite/whorled. There is also no mealy dusting; the surface is a flat gradient wash. The organism-level read fails here alone: these are conifer/bottlebrush needles-to-leaflets, not Chenopodium.

MUST-READ 2, CHUNKY TERMINAL SEED HEAD IN HOT COLOURS - PRESENT BUT UNREADABLE. Correcting the judge slightly: a hot colour IS on the canvas and it IS in the right place. Above the top rosette there is a vertical strand of roughly 9 small vermilion/orange-red beads. But it is ONE BEAD WIDE - about 5px across against a 150px-wide plant - roughly 45px tall, unbranched, and it reads as a thin antenna or a caterpillar's feeler rather than as a panicle. The packet asks for 'a dense branched panicle of tiny seeds' and 'chunky'. There is no branching, no mass, no width, and it carries maybe 1% of the silhouette area. So the judge's phrase 'a single thin red bead thread' is literally correct; the only correction is that they implied the identity carrier is effectively missing, when in fact the correct hue and position are already established and only the mass/branching are missing. That is the cheapest fix available: widen the panicle to 3-5 bead columns, branch it, and give it 20-25% of the plant height.

MUST-READ 3, GROOVED STRIPED STEM - ABSENT (the judge did not mention this at all). At 8x the stem is a single flat olive rectangle of perfectly uniform width running from the bottom whorl down toward the shadow. Zero grooves, zero longitudinal stripes, zero ridging, zero colour variation, and it terminates in a blunt square-cut end that hovers ABOVE the ground shadow ellipse rather than meeting it. It also does not continue up through the foliage - no stem is visible anywhere inside the column, so the whorls appear to float on nothing.

OTHER. Colour is a washed pale sage/khaki-cream throughout, not the packet's 'mid green'; there is no red or gold ripening tint on the foliage (optional, so not counted against it). Aspect measures ~0.65 against a spec of 0.5, close enough to ignore. Silhouette is perfectly bilaterally mirrored with no asymmetry or overlap, which is what makes it read as a manufactured chassis.

VERDICT. Two of three must-reads are flatly absent (duck-foot leaf, grooved striped stem) and the third is present in hue and position but at a tenth of the required mass and with no branching. The asset reads as the wrong organism - a bottlebrush/conifer spike with a red feeler - so FAIL is upheld.

rows.readsAs: a green ornamental fountain grass with a screw in it
rows.defect: All three must-reads fail simultaneously. The seed head is bolt upright on a stiff culm instead of arching over and nodding under its own weight. It is a compact ribbed ear with a flared cap — explicitly the thing the reference rules out — rather than a loose branched panicle. And there is no water, no flooded ground and no clump of several separate tillers; it is one solid fountain from a single point on dry shadow. Identical chassis and identical head to Barley, Millet, Oats, Rye and Sorghum, recoloured green.
rows.fix: Bend the panicle over into a heavy nodding arch of loose branched grain and stand two or three separate tillers in a visible waterline.
rows.verifyWhy:
Looked hard at the head, the base and the silhouette edge at 8x and 5x zoom. All three must-reads are absent and the FAIL stands; two parts of the stated cause need correcting, and there are two further defects the first judge did not name.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A single wide radial fountain of ~20 long narrow blades, bright grass-green with a lighter central highlight stripe per blade, springing from ONE point at ground level. Out of the middle of it rises one thin straight green culm carrying a pale straw-coloured seed glyph, and beneath the crown sits the standard dark elliptical drop-shadow.

MUST-READ 1 — 'nodding arching seed head bent under its own weight': ABSENT, and the judge's word 'bolt upright' is exactly right. At 8x the culm is dead vertical, the seed head is a perfectly straight-sided rectangular column with no lean, no curve and no tip droop whatsoever. There is not even a token bend at the neck. The whole point of rice — the head hanging over like a shepherd's crook — is nowhere on the canvas.

MUST-READ 3 — 'loose branched panicle, not a compact ear': ABSENT, and again the judge is right, though I can describe it more precisely so the fix has something to aim at. The head is TWO tight vertical ranks of small tan lozenge-shaped grains flanking a dark central rachis line — a two-ranked spike about 6px wide by 40px tall, zero branching, zero pedicels, zero spread. It is not merely compact, it is geometrically regular: the grains are stamped at even intervals in two mirrored columns. On top of it sits a hard-edged inverted trapezoid / funnel flare, wider than the whole head and flat across its top edge. That cap is not a plant part at all — at 8x it reads as a screw head or a champagne flute, a mechanical glyph with straight machined edges. THIS IS A NEW FINDING the first judge did not mention and it is arguably worse than the missing branching, because it actively reads as non-botanical.

MUST-READ 2 — 'clump of several stems standing in flooded ground': ABSENT in BOTH halves. (a) No water: I checked the whole lower third at 5x. The ground plane is the generic dark ellipse shadow used across the family; there is no water surface, no horizon/waterline crossing the culms, no reflection, no ripple, no colour shift at the base. (b) No clump: every blade converges to a SINGLE point — the crown is one narrow wedge tapering to a ~4px tip on the ground. There are no separate tillers, no offset crowns, no second or third culm. The plant is one rosette, not a stand.

CORRECTING THE CLAIM — 'just the shared fountain recoloured green' is LITERALLY true, and I verified it rather than assuming it: I opened Rye.png from the same batch. Rye is pixel-for-pixel the same radial fountain silhouette AND the same seed glyph — same funnel cap, same two-ranked grain column, same straight culm — simply recoloured straw-gold instead of green. So Rice and Rye are one chassis with a hue swap. That means the fix is not a Rice tweak; the grass chassis itself has no per-species head model.

SECOND NEW FINDING — ASPECT IS BADLY WRONG. Packet asks aspect 0.4 (tall and narrow). Measured ink bounding box is x 51..366, y 94..331 = 315 wide x 237 tall, aspect w/h = 1.33. The asset is more than three times wider relative to its height than specified; the fountain sprawls almost the full canvas width while the plant is short. Rye (spec 0.22, i.e. very tall thin culm) has the same sprawl, confirming the chassis ignores the aspect field entirely.

VERDICT: FAIL upheld. Nothing in this image distinguishes rice from any other generic grass, and the seed head reads as hardware rather than grain. Fixes needed, in priority order: (1) give the grass chassis a real panicle model — branched, drooping, arching over at the neck, and delete the trapezoid funnel cap; (2) split the crown into 3-5 separate tillers with distinct bases; (3) add a flooded-ground plane with a waterline across the lower culms; (4) honour the aspect field so the silhouette is tall rather than fan-wide.

rows.readsAs: a gold grass clump — indistinguishable from the Barley asset
rows.defect: Placed beside Barley this is the same picture: same fountain, same drooping outer blades, same short ribbed ear with a flared cap, same gold. The reference's whole point is that rye is taller and THINNER than wheat at aspect 0.22, yet the drawn silhouette is as wide as it is tall. The very long hair-fine awns are absent, the ear does not lean over at the tip, and the distinctly blue-green waxy bloom of rye foliage is nowhere — the leaves are the same gold as Barley's.

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked hard at the full 440x440 render, then at 7x and 14x nearest-neighbour crops of the ear, and measured ink bbox and mean foliage colour against the Barley asset. The FAIL stands, but three parts of the stated cause need correcting.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a single symmetric fountain/pampas-grass rosette. ~28 narrow blades all radiate from ONE point at ground level, arcing out and drooping at the tips, over a flat black elliptical ground shadow. There is no tall thin culm, no jointed nodes, no separate tillers - the blades are the whole plant and a single vertical stem rises from the exact centre of the rosette carrying ONE ear. The ear (approx x=215-245, y=110-165 in a 440px frame) is a straight vertical column of stacked chevron/herringbone grain marks split by a dark central groove, capped by a SOLID flat-topped inverted-triangle funnel (approx 30px wide, 25px tall). The whole ear+cap glyph reads as a machine screw / flathead bolt, or a lit torch, not as a cereal head.

CORRECTION 1 - 'no hair-fine awns' is imprecise. An awn TOKEN is present: the solid inverted-triangle funnel at the ear tip. It is not absent, it is the WRONG PRIMITIVE. It is a filled opaque wedge with only faint vertical banding, it flares upward from the tip only (it does not radiate along the flanks of the ear), and at ~25px it is roughly 40% of the 60px ear length rather than longer than the head. The fix is to replace that solid wedge with a splayed sheaf of individual 1px hair-fine strokes 1.5-2x the ear length, not to 'add awns' to a bare ear.

CORRECTION 2 - 'as wide as it is tall' understates it. Measured ink bbox (background-delta threshold, bg 5,6,12): Rye spans x 43-387, y 103-322 = 345w x 220h, aspect 1.57. Spec is 0.22. The asset is about 7x too wide for spec, and it is in fact WIDER than the Barley asset next to it (Barley 293w x 216h, aspect 1.36) - so the one species whose whole identity is 'taller and thinner than wheat' is the widest, squattest silhouette in the group (Wheat measures 324w x 198h). All three mustReads fail on this alone.

CORRECTION 3 - 'leaning ear tip' absent: CONFIRMED by pixel inspection. The ear column is perfectly vertical and bilaterally symmetric about its dark central groove, and the funnel cap sits square and level on top. Zero nod, zero lean, zero curvature anywhere in the stem.

COLOUR: confirmed by sampling. Mean foliage RGB over the blade mass is 126,114,73 for Rye vs 139,125,72 for Barley - both warm khaki-gold with R>G>B. There is not one blue-green or waxy-bloom pixel anywhere in the asset, and it is not even the grey-straw of the ripe state; it is the same warm gold as Barley.

BARLEY COMPARISON: the claim of indistinguishability holds for every identity-bearing element. Same rosette construction, same ground shadow, same single central stem, same chevron-column ear, same solid funnel cap, same palette. The only differences are non-semantic: Rye's blade fan splays wider and flatter (345px vs 293px) and its ear is a few pixels narrower. Swap the filenames and no viewer could tell which was which - and Barley's own mustRead (awns longer than the head, nodding when ripe) fails on the identical glyph, so this is one broken shared grain-head routine, not two independent misses.

BAND: FAIL. Three of three mustReads are absent (not tall/thin - it is wider than tall; ear does not lean; awns are a solid wedge, not long hair-fine bristles), the defining blue-green waxy leaf colour is absent, and the asset is a duplicate of a sibling species. Nothing here reads as rye.

rows.readsAs: an olive ornamental grass with a rust-coloured screw
rows.defect: Sorghum's reference asks for a tall THICK corn-like jointed cane with broad arching blades and a pale midrib, crowned by a heavy compact head. What is drawn is the same fine-bladed fountain as the other five grasses with no cane visible at all, blades that are narrow and midrib-free, and a head that is the same small ribbed cylinder and flared cap — the opposite of heavy or crowning. rows.fix: Give it a stout visible jointed cane with broad white-midribbed arching blades and crown it with a fat dense red-brown grain head several times the current size.
rows.verifyWhy:
FAIL upheld, with corrections. What I saw at 440px and at 6-10x crops of the head, mid-clump, a single blade, and the stem base:

SILHOUETTE / CHASSIS. The plant is a symmetrical tussock fountain: ~24 narrow ribbon blades all radiating from ONE point at soil level, arching out and down to left and right, widest at about 60% height. Behind them a single hairline culm runs dead-straight from that same ground point to the top. Must-read 1 (tall thick corn-like stem) is genuinely absent, and the judge's phrasing understates how absent: the culm is a uniform ~3px olive wire that does not thicken toward the base, has NO nodes, NO joints, NO sheath swellings anywhere along its length, and no taper. The packet's leaf spec is 'long broad arching blades ALTERNATING UP a stout jointed cane' - not one blade attaches above ground level, so the alternating-up-a-cane arrangement fails as well as the cane itself. For contrast, Corn.png in the same folder already has exactly the required chassis (thick green segmented cane with visible node rings and broad blades stepping alternately up it), so the correct chassis exists in the engine and was simply not used here.

BLADES / MIDRIB. Blades are 4-6px narrow ribbons in khaki-to-tan gold, shaded with a soft one-sided gradient (slightly lighter core, darker lower edge). There is NO pale or whitish midrib line on any blade; the darker lines visible between blades at 10x are the gaps where one blade overlaps another, not veins. Must-read 2 (broad arching blades with a white midrib) fails on both halves - not broad, no midrib. Colour is also off spec: packet asks mid green with a whitish midrib, render is uniform dry khaki/straw-gold.

HEAD - this is where the judge's description needs correcting. The head is NOT missing and is not merely 'small'; it is proportionally the same size as Millet's. It is a ~55px vertical element at the top of the culm made of two parts: (a) a threaded shank - a narrow parallel-sided rust-orange cylinder crossed by ~10 dark horizontal rungs, reading exactly like screw thread or a ladder, and (b) crowning it an inverted trapezoid that FLARES OUTWARD AS IT RISES to a flat top, i.e. a countersunk screw head / funnel. So the defect is not size but geometry: a grain head must be widest low-to-middle and taper to a point, and it must be dense; this one is a bare skinny spike that gets WIDER at the very top and is flat-cut across. It reads as hardware, not as 'a dense upright head of red-brown grain'. Must-read 3 (heavy compact seed head crowning the stem) is present in position and colour only; it fails on mass and shape.

MILLET COMPARISON. The judge's 'only a rust tint separates it from Millet' is close but not complete. Side by side, Sorghum and Millet share the identical chassis, identical blade count and fountain geometry, and the identical two-part screw head. The differences are: Sorghum is rendered ~1.6x larger with flatter, more widely arching blades, its foliage is rust-khaki where Millet is yellow-green, and its head is orange-rust where Millet's is pale gold. Scale and arch angle, not tint alone.

Band: FAIL. Two of three must-reads are wholly absent and the third is wrong in shape; the asset reads as a generic ornamental fountain grass with a screw stuck in it, not as sorghum.

rows.readsAs: a generic bean or pea vine floating on a diagonal
rows.defect: The leaves are plain flat circles — neither heart-shaped nor three-lobed, so the leaf must-read is missed outright. The runner does not hug the ground or spread wide; it hangs on a single 45-degree diagonal across the frame with the lower end stopping in mid-air, which reads as a fragment of a climbing vine rather than a trailing groundcover. The smooth spindle-shaped tubers are entirely absent, and the purple flush on stems and veins is absent too (the stems are plain green). Nothing in the picture says root crop.
rows.fix: Lay the runners horizontally along the ground, cut the leaves as heart-shaped or three-lobed blades on long purple-flushed stalks, and expose two or three smooth tapering orange tubers at the crown.
rows.verifyWhy:
Verdict upheld, but two of the three stated causes are described wrongly and the fix list needs correcting.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CANVAS (440x440; ink bbox measured at x129-310, y97-340 = 182 wide x 244 TALL, so the silhouette is a vertical column, w/h = 0.75). A single green stem enters at the bottom-left leaf just above an elliptical ground shadow and climbs in a sinuous S / zigzag up to the top-right, where it does terminate in mid-air behind the topmost leaf. Seven near-circular leaves alternate off it. At almost every node there is a small dark-green COILED SPRING TENDRIL (clearly visible as a spiral ring beside the stem at the base node and at three nodes up the vine). Nine small flat lilac/mauve U-shaped blobs (flat top, rounded bottom, ~10px, unshaded, RGB roughly 200,150,215) sit in loose vertical runs of 3-4, drawn ON TOP of the leaf blades rather than on any stalk.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM:
1. 'single 45-degree diagonal' is wrong. The runner is a serpentine S-curve, not a straight diagonal, and its lower end does not hang in mid-air - it lands on the bottom-left leaf right at the cast shadow. The top end is the one that stops in mid-air. The real, damning geometry fact the claim missed is the ASPECT: the packet asks aspect 2 (twice as wide as tall, spreading along the ground) and the art is 0.75 (taller than wide). It is a CLIMBING vine, not a ground-hugging one. That is the must-read failure, not the diagonal.
2. 'plain flat circles' is not quite right either. The leaves are not plain - each carries a straight central midrib, four to six pinnate lateral veins, and a soft 3D gradient with a specular highlight. The defect is purely the OUTLINE: every leaf is an unbroken round-to-ovate disc with no cordate notch at the petiole and no lobing whatsoever. So 'heart-shaped or three-lobed leaves' genuinely fails, but the fix is the silhouette, not the shading.
3. 'smooth spindle tubers entirely absent' - a harvest element IS drawn, it just isn't a tuber. The nine lilac U-blobs occupy the harvest slot. They are the wrong shape (short blunt pips, not long tapering spindles), the wrong colour (pale mauve, not orange or purple-red), the wrong scale, and in the wrong place (floating on the leaf faces mid-vine instead of a cluster at the plant base). Nothing at all sits at or under the ground shadow - I zoomed the base region at 6x and there is bare shadow ellipse only. So the must-read fails, but the fix is 'replace the mauve pips with basal spindle tubers', not 'add missing geometry'.

ADDITIONAL DEFECT THE CLAIM DID NOT NAME, and the strongest single reason it reads as a bean/pea: the coiled spring tendrils. Sweet potato is a morning-glory relative - it TWINES, it has no tendrils at all. Tendrils are a legume/cucurbit cue and they are drawn at four visible nodes. They must be deleted.

Also missing: leafColour asks for a deep purple flush on stems and veins; stems and veins are uniform mid-green with no purple anywhere.

All three must-reads fail (no ground-hugging wide spread, no heart/lobed leaf, no smooth spindle tuber), plus an active false cue (tendrils). FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a clump of hosta or water-lily pads, or a green scallop shell / folding hand fan
rows.defect: All three must-reads are absent. The leaves are near-CIRCULAR paddles, not heart-shaped elephant ears, and every tip points sideways/upward around the fan arc — not one blade tip points down. There are no petioles anywhere: the seven blades emerge from a single buried point at the bottom centre with zero visible stalk, so the peltate 'stalk joins inside the blade, not at the notch' read cannot exist — there is no notch and no stalk to attach. No brown ringed corm, no fibrous hair, no purple flecking; the base of the plant is simply empty dark background. The whole thing is a flat overlapping shell of lens shapes with one straight centre-rib each, hugging the ground horizontally instead of standing up.
rows.fix: Rebuild it as 3-5 THICK UPRIGHT STALKS rising from a brown ringed corm sitting on the ground line, each stalk topped by a big heart-shaped blade hanging tip-DOWN with the stalk visibly inserted a third of the way into the blade face (peltate) rather than at the rim.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, 0 of 3 must-reads present. I read the 440x440 PNG, then re-read it at 3x and 8x zoom with brightness gain on the base, the leaf mass and the convergence point, and ran a per-pixel colour/bbox scan. What is actually drawn: a rosette of six to seven broad, near-circular to broadly-ovate blades overlapping like a hand of cards, all radiating from ONE bare point at approximately (218, 277). Plant bounding box is x 77..364, y 134..309 -- 288 wide by 176 tall, i.e. a landscape fan of aspect ~1.6 against a reference aspect of 1.0 for an upright herb. The entire lower 30 percent of the frame (y 310..440) is pure empty background.

MUST-READ 1, elephant-ear leaves pointing DOWNWARD: absent. Every blade carries a legible midrib running outward from the convergence point, and I traced them: the right-hand blade's midrib runs up-and-right to the frame's right edge, the upper blades' midribs run up and up-left, the left blades' run left and down-left only as far as horizontal. Not one tip is directed downward, and no blade is cordate -- there is no basal notch or heart lobe anywhere; the tips are blunt paddle ends, not the long drooping points of Colocasia. The judge's description of this defect is CORRECT.

MUST-READ 2, stalk joins the leaf INSIDE the blade (peltate): absent. I confirm the judge's conclusion but must refine the stated cause, because the fix is different. It is not that the blades lack internal linework -- each blade DOES have an internal midrib with lateral veins branching off it, clearly visible at 3x on the right-hand leaf. The failure is that every midrib originates at the blade's own basal EDGE, at the point where all blades meet, i.e. marginal attachment, exactly the non-peltate arrangement the reference forbids. Separately, and as the judge says, there are no petioles at all: at 8x on the convergence point the blades simply taper together to a bare vertex and the background begins immediately beneath it. There is no stalk segment, no thick upright petiole, nothing joining the rosette to anything below. So the peltate read fails twice over -- no stalk to insert, and the insertion line that does exist is at the edge.

MUST-READ 3, brown ringed corm at the base: absent, and confirmed numerically. A full-image scan classifying every non-background pixel found 38,780 greenish pixels and ZERO warm/brown pixels (test: R>G>B with R-B greater than 25) in the entire image. There is no corm, no fibrous hair, no ring texture, no soil line, and no ground plane of any kind. The judge's phrase 'the plant's base is empty background' is literally accurate.

One small correction to their gestalt: they call it 'a flat fan of hosta or lily pads LYING ON THE GROUND.' The organism read is right -- overlapping rounded discs radiating from a single low crown is a hosta/water-lily rosette -- but nothing is lying on ground, because no ground is drawn; the rosette floats with its vertex hanging over empty space. The colour is also cooler and more mint-toned than the reference's 'dull mid green with a matte water-beading surface,' with a strong pale specular wash across the upper blades rather than a matte beaded surface, which adds to the lily-pad reading.

Fix direction: rebuild as three to five separate tall petioles rising from a visible brown ringed corm at the frame bottom (roughly y 340..400), each petiole terminating INSIDE its blade well above the basal notch, with each blade hung so its long point droops downward; widen the vertical extent to fill the 1.0 aspect and drop the specular wash for a matte finish.

rows.readsAs: a golden ornamental fountain grass with a wood screw or a paintbrush ferrule stuck upright in the middle of it
rows.defect: The identity must-read — long stiff awn bristles fanning out from the ear — is absent. Zoomed in, the ear is a straight-sided ribbed COLUMN of tiny paired ticks that never break past the column's own width, capped by an inverted trapezoid flare; it reads unmistakably as a flat-head screw thread, not a grain ear. Nothing radiates. The second must-read also fails: instead of a single unbranched straw with a few widely spaced flat leaves, the plant is a dense tussock of roughly sixteen narrow arching blades all sprung from one point, with only one culm carrying a head — that is pampas/ornamental grass silhouette, not a wheat plant. No jointed culm, no leaf sheaths clasping it, no blue-green-to-gold ripening gradient.
rows.fix: Redraw the ear as a short plump spikelet body with 15-25 LONG straight awn bristles sweeping up and outward well beyond the ear's own width in a V-shaped spray, and cut the tussock down to one upright jointed straw carrying three or four widely spaced flat leaves.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD. I read the 440x440 PNG, then re-cropped and nearest-neighbour upscaled the ear (x180-270,y70-200 at 8x) and the foliage (x20-420,y150-350 at 3x) and looked at both.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN. A single thin olive-green culm rises from a dense radiating fountain of blades. At the culm's top sits an ear occupying only y~95-165 (about 70px of a ~215px-tall plant, so roughly a quarter of the plant's height). The ear is a perfectly straight-sided vertical rectangle about 12px wide with NO taper, NO shoulder and NO apex point. Inside it is a ladder of ~14 tiny paired chevron ticks arranged in two columns either side of a dark central channel. Capping it is a SOLID FILLED inverted trapezoid, widest at the very top, about 2.5x the ear's width, with a flat top edge and clean straight diagonal sides. Together the threaded shaft plus countersunk flat cap read unmistakably as a flat-head wood screw or a paintbrush ferrule. The judge's description of this is accurate.

AWNS - CONFIRMED ABSENT. I specifically hunted for small or misplaced bristles. Nothing radiates past the ear's own 12px width anywhere along its length; every spikelet tick terminates inside the column outline. The only bristle-like marks in the whole asset are two or three ~4px angled tips at the very BASE of the ear pointing DOWN-and-outward - the wrong direction entirely (real awns sweep steeply upward from each spikelet, well past the ear width and typically as long again as the ear). PARTIAL CORRECTION TO THE CLAIM: the top trapezoid is plausibly a collapsed attempt at an awn fan - it is in the right place and has the right outward splay - but it is rendered as one solid filled polygon with no internal line separation, so it reads as a machined flange, not as bristles. That is the specific fix: it must become 15-25 discrete straight stiff lines, each 0.6-1.0x the ear length, emerging from the spikelets along the WHOLE ear and splaying only slightly, not one solid cap at the tip.

SINGLE UNBRANCHED STRAW - CONFIRMED FAILED, with a count correction. The judge said sixteen blades; I count roughly 18-20 arching blades erupting from one basal point and recurving hard to the sides. The plant's bounding box is about 365px wide by 215px tall - an aspect near 1.7 - against the reference row's aspect: 0.25 (i.e. it should be nearly four times taller than wide). It is off by about 7x in the wrong direction. The reference leaf line asks for 'few and widely spaced' flat blades clasping the culm; what is drawn is a dense continuous skirt with no gaps and no clasping joints, and the blades arch/droop rather than standing stiff. 'Golden pampas grass / fountain grass with one head' is a fair read; I would add dracaena or a spider plant as equally likely reads.

WHAT DOES PASS: the ear is stiff and upright, not drooping (that must-read is met), the colour is correct gold-straw with a green culm, and the ground shadow and lighting are clean. Nothing else rescues it - two of three must-reads fail and the ear reads as hardware, so FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: a thin unsupported bean or morning-glory vine
rows.defect: No support at all — the must-read is a woody stem CLINGING to a pole/trunk with root pads, and the vine floats free with nothing to climb. Leaves are small narrow lance blades, not the broad ribbed heart-shaped leaves that are pepper's main tell. The fruit strings are two short colourless grey-white bead threads, not drooping green-to-red peppercorn catkins, and read as fungus or scale insects.
rows.fix: Draw a brown trunk/pole up the frame with the stem wrapped on it and visible root pads, swap the lance leaves for broad heart-shaped leaves with curved parallel ribs, and recolour the hanging spikes green-through-red.
rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, but two parts of the stated cause are wrong and would send the fix in the wrong direction. What is actually on canvas (440x440, subject bbox x135-303 y102-324, aspect 0.76 vs spec 0.7 - fine): a single sinuous S-curving mid-green cord climbing from a ground-shadow ellipse to the top, ~14 leaf blades alternating off it, ~7 dark loops, and two white bead spikes. Nothing else is drawn.

1) SUPPORT - the judge is right and I verified it. There is no pole, trunk, trellis or neighbouring stem anywhere in the frame; the only non-vine mark is the flat shadow ellipse. The stem does not even reach the ground: at the base (crop 180,260 130x80) it terminates as a blunt rounded green tip floating ~8px ABOVE the shadow, with no root flare, no soil mound, no basal collar. At the top it likewise ends in mid-air. So it reads as a cut length of vine hanging in space.

2) CLINGING ORGANS - the judge's 'no root pads' is technically true but he MISSED the seven organs that ARE drawn, and the fix depends on knowing they exist. Alternating with the leaves along the whole stem are seven dark-green (RGB ~30,63,24) outlined loops, ~18px across. At 16x (crop 165,95) they resolve unambiguously as SPIRAL TENDRIL COILS - an open hook that curls into an inner spiral, exactly the pea/grape/passionflower organ. They are the wrong clinging organ for Piper nigrum, which climbs by short bristly adventitious rootlets pressed flat along a host trunk, and they grip nothing - every coil closes on empty background. So the fix is NOT 'add clinging organs to a bare stem'; it is 'delete the seven tendril spirals, replace with a dense band of short stubby rootlets on the support-facing side of each node, and draw a host trunk/pole for them to grip.'

3) LEAVES - the judge is right. Every blade is a narrow lanceolate lance roughly 40x9px (~4.5:1) with a single straight pale midline highlight and NO curved parallel secondary ribs, sharp-pointed at both ends, no cordate/heart base, no basal lobes at all. Read together with the coiling stem the silhouette is willow- or bamboo-like. Two further misses the judge did not name: the packet asks for 'dark glossy green' and the lit blades render as a light spring green (up to ~150,220,160) with a soft airbrush gradient rather than a glossy dark leaf; and the packet's 'woody stem' is absent - the stem is a smooth uniform herbaceous green cord with no bark, no lenticels, no swollen nodes.

4) FRUIT - the judge is HALF WRONG here and this is the part that must be corrected. The colour half of his claim is exactly right and I confirmed it numerically: I scanned the whole canopy box (63,000 opaque px, y60-270 x60-360) for reddish pixels (r>g+25 and r>b+25) and found ZERO. Not one red or orange pixel exists in the asset. The 345 bright bead pixels cluster at RGB ~(148,159,153) / (144,147,149) - a flat grey-white with only a faint green cast - so the 'green-to-red round peppercorns' ramp is entirely missing and the beads do read as a crust of scale insects or mealybugs on the stem. BUT his structural implication ('bead threads' stuck on) is wrong: at 16x (crop 165,165) each is a genuine PENDULOUS SPIKE - a dark-green rachis hanging down and away from a leaf node, with ~20 small round berries packed alternately along both sides of it and a bare tip. The bright-pixel column profile isolates exactly two of them, x177-186 and x249-259, each ~26px long. So the third must-read, 'drooping catkin-like strings of berries', is STRUCTURALLY PRESENT AND CORRECT - it fails on colour and on the blown-out all-specular shading only. The fix is a recolour (matte body ramping green->orange->red down the spike, one small specular dot per berry, berry edge darker than centre), not a re-draw.

VERDICT: of the three must-reads, one (catkin spikes) is present and only mis-coloured, and two (woody stem clinging to a support with root pads; heart-shaped ribbed leaves) are absent. With lance leaves, free-air tendril spirals and white beads, the asset reads as a generic willow-leaved twining vine with an insect infestation - it is not identifiable as black pepper, and could be swapped for half the climbers in the set. FAIL stands.

rows.readsAs: an agave or dwarf fan palm

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: roughly 19 perfectly straight, stiff, lance/spike blades radiating fanwise across about 180 degrees from ONE common point at soil level. Every blade shares that single node — measured green bbox is x88..352, y142..287, i.e. 265 wide x 146 tall (w/h ~1.81) against a packet aspect of 0.8, so the silhouette is nearly wide where it should be tall. MUST-READ 1 'tall arching leafy canes from a clump' — ABSENT. There is not one cane, stem, sheath or node anywhere in the image; no leaf arches, all are dead-straight rays; there is no clump (multiple shoot bases), only a single convergence point. Two-ranked leaf arrangement is impossible to read from a radial rosette.

MUST-READ 2 'a separate low flowering shoot snaking along the ground' — ABSENT. The 4.5x brightness lift confirms the region below the rosette contains nothing but a plain elliptical drop shadow: no stalk, no bracts, no flower, no dark shape masked by the shadow. rows.readsAs: a generic tree infested with brown caterpillars

rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, and the chassis diagnosis is right, but several specifics in the claim need correcting.

WHAT I SAW (440x440, measured on pixels). Silhouette: a bare unbranched trunk, constant 27px wide, running from the ground shadow at y=374 up to y=215 -- that is ~160px of the plant's 305px total height, more than half the organism, with a rounded cap end and NO branch structure whatsoever. Above it a single soft green cloud blob. Measured green bbox is x86..346, y69..215: crown 246px wide x 146px tall, ratio 1.7:1 WIDER THAN TALL, and the widest rows are y159-y189, i.e. the LOWER third. I opened Cinnamon.png side by side: identical chassis -- same bare capsule trunk, same oblate green cloud, same scattered lance leaves, differing ONLY in the brown decoration sprinkled on the cloud (rosettes for Cinnamon, strings for Clove). The judge's 'same trunk-plus-cloud chassis as Cinnamon' is CONFIRMED.

CORRECTION 1 -- COUNT. There are FIVE bud strings, not four. Column-scanning the red-dominant pixels gives distinct stacks at x=149-156, x=180-191 (which carries TWO strings stacked one above the other, upper y~100-140 and lower y~155-200), x=256-263 and x=294-300. Any fix must move these into a pink-red/crimson range distinct from the trunk, not just add bumps.

CORRECTION 3 -- SHAPE AND PLACEMENT. At 7x zoom each string is a vertical column of 8-10 FLAT, EVENLY-SIZED, OVERLAPPING CIRCLES -- a bead chain / bottlebrush / string-of-berries. 'Caterpillar' is a fair reading and so is 'blackberry on a stick'. What is missing is the nail form: a clove bud is a slender tapering shaft with a swollen four-pointed calyx head, and there is not one tapering or headed element in the image. Equally important and NOT mentioned by the first judge: the strings hang free INSIDE the crown mass, several of them descending toward the trunk, and since the trunk is unbranched there are no branch tips for them to sit on. 'TERMINAL sprays' therefore cannot read even in principle -- the fix needs branch tips before it needs bud shapes. MUST-READ 3 ABSENT.

WHERE THE FIRST JUDGE UNDERSOLD THE ASSET. The leaves are genuinely better than a FAIL implies and should not be rebuilt: they are true lance blades (pointed at both ends, ~4:1, with a lighter midrib stroke), mid-to-bright green #3C7F46 over a darker cloud, ~30 of them fringing the blob. VERDICT. Two of three must-reads are absent (conical crown; terminal nail-shaped bud sprays), the third only half-present, and the asset is a palette-swap of Cinnamon down to the trunk geometry. It reads as a generic brown-fruited shade tree. FAIL stands.

FIX ORDER: (1) rebuild the crown as tall narrow cone, height ~2x width, apex at top, widest near the base -- this alone separates it from Cinnamon; (2) give the trunk 4-6 forking branches whose tips exit the crown silhouette; (3) replace bead chains with 5-9 tapering nail-shaped buds radiating from a single point at each branch tip, in pink-red/crimson clearly off the trunk hue; (4) pair the lance leaves at opposite nodes along the branches and tint the outermost few bronze.

rows.readsAs: a young conifer or a hemp plant
rows.defect: The must-read is ONE stem topped by a SINGLE whorl of five-fingered leaves; the render stacks about ten palmate whorls the full height of the stem into a dense column, which destroys the diagnostic architecture entirely. rows.verifyWhy:
Upheld, and the core of the claim is confirmed at 5x zoom on the top, mid and base crops, with three corrections/additions to the stated cause.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRAWN: a single straight dark-green stem carrying a continuous column of leaf whorls stacked from y=105 to y=313 out of a 440px canvas. Each tier is a semicircular FAN of roughly 12-16 narrow lanceolate, saw-toothed leaflets radiating from a single hub directly on the stem, with no petiole; each fan overlaps the one below so the silhouette is a solid conifer-shaped column with a serrated edge. Per-row width analysis shows a periodic bulge every ~12px over the 208px of foliage; visually about 10-12 fans are separately readable. The read is unambiguously a young spruce/hemlock or a cannabis spike - not a ginseng.

MUST-READ 1, 'a single stem topped by a whorl of five-fingered leaves': FAILED, but note the precise defect for the fix. It is not that the leaflets are the wrong shape - they are narrow and toothed, which is close enough to a ginseng leaflet. The two defects are (a) there is no SINGLE CROWN whorl: the whorl motif is repeated up the entire stem, so the plant has ~10+ whorls instead of one; and (b) each whorl is a fan of 12-16 leaflets fused at one hub, not 3-4 LONG-STALKED palmate leaves each bearing FIVE leaflets. Ginseng's silhouette depends on visible leaf STALKS separating the crown into a few five-fingered hands; there are zero petioles anywhere in this render.

MUST-READ 2, 'a small cluster of red berries in the centre of the whorl': PARTIALLY present, and the judge's description needs a correction. The berries ARE drawn and are readable - a tight head of about ten scarlet spheres with pale specular highlights, correctly sized and correctly coloured, at y~95-125. They sit ON TOP of the uppermost leaf fan rather than nested in the centre of a crown, exactly as claimed. What the judge missed: a bare green stem tip continues UPWARD past the berries to y=84, so the cluster is impaled mid-stem rather than terminal, which makes it read as a berry bead threaded on an axis rather than an umbel held in a leaf crown. The berries are the only must-read element that is nearly right; keep them, and re-site them into the centre of a single crown whorl and terminate the stem at the cluster.

MUST-READ 3, 'the pale branching root': ABSENT, confirmed. The base crop shows a 3-4px wide plain green stem running from the lowest fan straight down into the shadow ellipse. There is no swelling, no colour change to pale buff, no fork, no rootlets - nothing at all below the foliage but stem. The forked man-shaped root is the single most identifying feature of ginseng and it is not drawn.

ADDITIONAL DEFECT THE JUDGE DID NOT NAME: aspect. The packet specifies aspect 0.9 (near square). The rendered non-background bounding box is 67 x 259 px, aspect 0.259 - roughly 3.5x too tall and narrow. The column form is therefore not only wrong in motif but also violates the stated silhouette proportion, and fixing the whorl-stacking to a single crown would move the aspect back toward spec on its own.

MINOR: leaf colour reads as a pale greyish sage with dark speckle marks rather than the specified mid green, though this is a polish-level note and not the reason for the band.

rows.readsAs: lavender, or a bundle of dead twigs with purple tips

rows.readsAs: a willowherb or vetch weed with a lilac tip
rows.defect: Every leaf is a smooth narrow untoothed lance — mint's identity is a paired TOOTHED OVAL leaf and it is absent, so the plant reads as a different genus. The stem is a plain round green line with no square section and no flat faces, and the pairs sit flat in one plane rather than crossing at right angles at each node. Only the small lilac bead spike is right. The drawing is the Chamomile/Echinacea/Oregano ladder with a lilac tip.

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG at 1x, then re-cropped and magnified four regions (whole plant 3x brightened, a single node 8x, the bare lower stem 12x, the flower tip 10x) and sampled raw pixel rows across the stem. What is actually on canvas: a single unbranched vertical stalk running from a bare point at the soil shadow to the top of frame, carrying NINE nodes of leaves, then continuing as a naked stalk for ~55px above the top leaf pair, capped by a terminal spike of ~8 stacked pale-lilac beads (approx rgb 190,175,220). FAIL UPHELD - the asset reads as a pinnate frond (vetch / acacia / false-indigo), not as a mint sprig. But three parts of the stated cause are wrong and a fix made against them would miss.

(1) WRONG: 'paired leaves crossing at each node are absent'. The PAIRING is present and clean. At 8x every node carries EXACTLY TWO leaves, one left one right, attaching at the identical y on the stem - true opposite phyllotaxy, nine tidy pairs. What is absent is the DECUSSATE CROSSING: both leaves of every pair are drawn at full length in the picture plane, and every pair is identical to every other, so there is no alternating near-pair / foreshortened-pair rhythm. The result is one flat ladder that the eye parses as a single compound frond. The fix is not 'add pairs', it is 'alternate the pairs: draw every other node as a short foreshortened pair (or a pair of near-circular face-on discs) so the 90-degree turn is visible'.

(2) CORRECT AND CENTRAL: leaf shape. Every one of the 18 blades is a smooth linear lance about 45px long by 8px wide (~5.5:1) with a single pale midrib streak, a needle-sharp tip and a perfectly clean margin - zero serration anywhere on the silhouette at 9x. Mint needs a ~2:1 toothed oval with a rounded base and a visibly saw-edged margin. This alone destroys the read.

(3) WRONG DESCRIPTION, RIGHT CONCLUSION: 'plain round green stem'. The stem is not round-shaded at all. Pixel rows at y=200/250/300/330 show it is a flat 4px-wide bar of one uniform colour (rgb 39,91,31) with no gradient, no rim light, no cylinder shading and no facet or corner ridge. So the square-stem must-read is indeed ABSENT, but the fix is not 'flatten a cylinder' - it is 'widen the stem and give it two tone-separated faces plus a hard vertical corner highlight so the four-sided section is legible', plus node swellings where the pairs attach (there are none; the leaves emerge from a featureless bar).

(4) NOT MENTIONED BY THE JUDGE, AND IT PASSES: must-read 3, 'terminal spikes of small pale purple flowers', is present and readable - a beaded lilac column at the very tip. Keep it. But it currently sits on a long naked stalk held well clear of the foliage, which is the LAVENDER silhouette (item 9 in this same batch: 'long naked stalk with a short dense violet spike at the tip'). I opened Lavender.png to check for a shared chassis - it is genuinely different (a multi-stem woody bush of five brown stalks), so this is not a duplicate, but Mint's spike should be pulled down closer above the top leaf pair and given whorled/interrupted tiers rather than a smooth even bead column.

Also missing versus the packet row: no purple-tinged leaf variant, no basal/soil detail (the stem just tapers to a point at the shadow), and the plant is a lone stem where mint is a leafy multi-stem clump. Score: 1 of 3 must-reads present (flower spike), 1 half-present (pairing yes, toothed oval and crossing no), 1 absent (square stem). Band FAIL is correct; this is a shape rebuild, not a polish.

Net: the asset does not read as Mustard or as any brassica. It reads as a bottlebrush/horsetail with a dandelion head stuck on. FAIL stands. Fix direction: this needs a new chassis, not a retouch — a branching herb with a big end-lobed basal leaf at the base, an open corymb of individually-drawn four-petal yellow crosses at each branch tip (each floret needs to be at least ~8-10 px so the cross is readable), and a ring of slender pods angling outward and upward from the stem immediately below each flower cluster.
