rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG at full size, then decoded it and re-rendered three crops (body 3x, whole frame 2x contrast-stretched, bottom edge 4x contrast-stretched) to hunt for small features. The FAIL stands, but two of its stated causes are wrong and the fix should not be aimed at them.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE: a single irregular convex polygon, roughly 12-sided, about 210px wide by 145px tall, sitting centred and slightly above the vertical middle. Its widest axis is horizontal and it tapers to a blunt point on the right, which is what gives the 'wedge' read. Fill is pale blue-grey / ice white with a faint cyan cast, not neutral grey. Silhouette edges are hard, straight and faceted -- no soft organic curve anywhere on the outline. There is NO cap, NO stipe, NO rim or margin, NO gill radials, NO pore field, NO annulus, NO volva, NO substrate, NO ground-shadow ellipse. The bottom edge (verified at 4x with contrast stretch) is just another slightly wavy polygon segment terminating in empty background: the body floats, unanchored. Nothing in the drawing establishes which end is up.

CORRECTION 1 -- 'flat unshaded' is inaccurate. There IS shading: a large soft radial highlight is baked into the body, centred left-of-centre and roughly one third down, falling off toward all edges, and the facets carry faint gradient variation. The problem is not absence of shading, it is that the shading is a generic centred blob glow that describes no anatomy -- it does not build a cap dome, does not turn an underside into shadow, does not separate a head from a stalk. A fix that merely 'adds shading' will not move this asset.

CORRECTION 2 -- the outside speckles are NOT a render artifact and not 'loose spill'. Zoomed, they resolve into two deliberate layers: hard-edged white dots (2-5px, sharp, evenly scattered both inside and outside the body) and larger soft blurred bokeh puffs arranged in a clear elliptical ring that orbits the whole silhouette at a consistent standoff. That is an intentional spore-release halo, and it is the ONE element on the asset that carries any fungal signal at all. It should be kept, not deleted. The failure is that a spore halo alone cannot carry the identity when the thing releasing the spores has no fungal body.

BATCH COHERENCE (packet gives no reference row and asks for a sibling comparison, so I opened two): fungi-h1-s0 is an unmistakable morel/inky-cap -- tall diamond-textured conical cap, cream stipe of clearly different value, and a dark ground-shadow ellipse. fungi-h1-s18 is a puffball -- shaded sphere with radiating spines and a dark apical ostiole dot, again on a ground-shadow ellipse. Both siblings read instantly as fungi, both are anchored to ground, both have a shaded volumetric primary mass. s19 shares none of that: no fungal organ, no ground contact, faceted low-poly outline instead of an organic mass. It is an outlier against its own family, not the family norm.

VERDICT: the defining must-read (a recognisable fungal body -- cap+stipe, or a puffball/pore mass -- sitting on a substrate) is genuinely absent. At thumbnail scale this reads as a chunk of ice or a low-poly asteroid inside a dust cloud. FAIL upheld.

FIX DIRECTION: keep the spore halo and the pale spore dots; replace the faceted polygon with a curved, volumetrically shaded fungal mass (a puffball/earthstar body would suit the existing spore-burst motif better than a gilled cap), give it a top/bottom axis with an apical pore or a short stipe, and add the ground-shadow ellipse that every other member of this batch already has.

rows.readsAs: a small cratered moon or an ice planetoid

At 12x the ~30 marks are perfectly FLAT, uniform-fill grey-blue discs (~#a9b6c0 on a ~#dbe6f0 body) with a soft antialiased edge and ZERO interior modelling: no crescent shadow, no lit inner wall, no raised rim, no drop shadow. They have no depth cue at all, so they do not read as craters and they do not read as puffball warts either -- they read as flat printed polka dots / decals. Worse, they stay perfectly circular and the same size right out toward the limb (e.g. the pair at x~277,y~205 sits within a few px of the terminator edge and is still a full round disc) -- they never foreshorten or wrap the curvature, which actively FLATTENS the sphere into a dotted ball. The fix is not "make the pits less crater-like"; it is that the ornamentation carries no fungal information and no surface curvature.

CORRECTION 2 -- "the gradient as a planetary terminator" is WRONG. There is no terminator and no hard shadow side. It is a plain top-left key-light spherical gradient with a smooth, gentle falloff in every direction, plus a thin bright specular rim along the upper-right/right limb (that part of the claim is correct and clearly visible). "Floating over a cast ellipse" is also slightly overstated: the sphere's bottom arc does terminate INSIDE the soft dark cast ellipse (ellipse spans roughly y=255-292, body base y=281), so it is nominally grounded -- but there is no contact occlusion, no darkening where body meets ground, and the ellipse is a bare soft shadow over an empty warm radial vignette, so the grounding is weak and the ellipse contributes nothing to a fungal read.

WHY IT STILL FAILS, ON COHERENCE. Judged against its own batch, this is the one member with no fungal cue at all. fungi-h1-s5 and s6 use the SAME sphere chassis but carry two identity-bearing features -- radiating spines plus a single dark central apical pore -- and both consequently read as puffballs (Lycoperdon). fungi-h1-s7 is a lobed golden mass hanging off a curved brown branch, i.e. body + explicit substrate. fungi-h1-s8 is a clump of violet coral-fungus fingers. s4 is the s5/s6 chassis with BOTH of the identity features deleted (no spines, and critically no ostiole) and replaced by depthless dots. What remains is a bare sphere, and its palette is the coldest and least organic in the batch -- pale ice-blue/white against the siblings' saturated teal, gold and violet -- so the residual read is astronomical, not fungal. The judge's "cratered moon" gestalt call is right even though the crater and terminator mechanisms cited are not.

SMALLEST SUFFICIENT FIX: restore the apical pore/ostiole that s5 and s6 already have, add a narrowed sterile base with contact shading so the body meets ground instead of hovering on a detached ellipse, and re-render the surface marks as raised warts with a lit top edge and a small drop shadow that foreshorten toward the limb. Warming the pale blue off pure lunar white would also help. Body scale (~32% canvas width) is undersized relative to s8 as a secondary note.

rows.verifyWhy:
Looked at the 440x440 PNG, then re-cropped and upscaled the body region 4x and the lower-left quadrant 8x to check spike bases and ground contact. The verdict stands but four of the five stated causes are wrong and would send a fix in the wrong direction.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE: a single smooth teal sphere (~110px diameter, centred ~x218/y205), lit from upper-left with a soft radial-gradient highlight at about 10 o'clock and no rim light, no surface texture of any kind — no speckle, no warts, no scales, no pores, no reticulation. Radiating from it are SEVEN (not eight) flat triangular spikes. Counting clockwise from top: ~11:30 short, ~1:30 long, ~3:00 long, ~4:30 medium, ~6:00 short (points down-left into the shadow), ~8:00 long, ~9:30 long. They are NOT at even angles — gaps run from roughly 35deg (1:30 to 3:00) to roughly 60deg (6:00 to 8:00), and the two left spikes sit almost parallel as a visible pair. Lengths are NOT uniform either: the 9:30 and 8:00 spikes run about 60px, the 11:30 and 6:00 spikes about 20px, a 3x spread. One small dark disc (~9px, flat, slightly darker teal, no rim, no depression, no highlight) sits ABOVE AND LEFT of the sphere's geometric centre. Beneath everything is a large soft cast-shadow ellipse about 1.9x the body's width.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM:
1. 'Eight ... at even angles' is wrong twice — there are seven, at visibly irregular spacing with a bare arc on the lower-left and a near-parallel pair on the left.
2. 'Needle lances' with 'no organic base swelling' is wrong. At 8x the spikes are broad-based isoceles wedges: the 6:00 spike's base spans roughly 22px where it meets the sphere, wider than a fifth of the body radius. The base widening IS present. The real defect at the join is different and more fixable: the wedge edges are perfectly straight, hard-aliased polygon edges with zero taper curvature, the join is a hard silhouette corner with no fillet or gradient blend into the body, and every spike is filled with one flat lighter-teal value that ignores the body's upper-left key light — the 8:00 spike (facing away from the light) is the same brightness as the 1:30 spike (facing into it). So: not 'missing base swelling' but 'flat unlit polygons pasted onto a shaded sphere'.
3. 'The body touches no substrate' is FALSE. There is a cast shadow ellipse and the sphere's lower edge sits well inside its upper half; the 6:00 spike descends into it. Ground contact reads fine. What is genuinely absent is BASAL ATTACHMENT — no stipe, no volva, no mycelial skirt, no rooting cord, no substrate texture. The sphere meets the ground on a single tangent point like a dropped ball, which is the fungally-wrong part.
4. 'Detonator port' overstates it. The dark dot is a flat offset disc with no rim, and at this scale it reads as a single cyclops EYE more than a fuze. It is also the one element that could have been saved: a puffball's apical ostiole would be exactly a central pore, but it needs to be ON the apex (this one is off-centre and on the upper-left face), and it needs a raised rim or an inset shadow to read as a hole rather than a pupil.

WHY IT STILL FAILS: the judge is right about the gestalt. Sphere plus seven long radiating lances is a naval contact mine / caltrop / sea urchin / virus-icon silhouette. Nothing in the asset carries a fungal must-read: no cap, no gill or pore underside, no stipe, no annulus, no volva, no spore texture, no clustering, no decaying substrate. Spiny puffballs (Lycoperdon echinatum, Sclerodermataceae) do exist, but their spines are DENSE, SHORT and SOFT and cover the whole surface — the opposite of seven sparse hard lances. Cross-checked against the batch: fungi-h1-s6 is this identical chassis recoloured cream (same sphere, same seven-spike arrangement, same offset dark dot), and fungi-h1-s4 is the same sphere with the spikes swapped for grey speckles. This is one generic procedural primitive — sphere + optional radiating spikes + optional dot — not a fungal form language, which is the batch-level 'do these share one body?' failure as well. The fix is structural (silhouette and basal attachment), not polish.

UPHELD, but three of the four specifics in the original claim are wrong and the fix must be aimed elsewhere than where they point.

WHAT I SAW. Packet reference row for fungi-h1-s6 is 'reference row: **NONE** (procedural or unlisted - judge coherence, and judge it against the others in this batch)', so there is no mustRead list; the batch header's own primary question governs: 'DO THESE SHARE ONE BODY?'. The asset is a glossy bone-white sphere, ball radius 44.0 px centred about (220,208) in a 440x440 frame, pierced by seven straight needle-sharp lances, with one small grey dot on the ball face and a soft black ground ellipse beneath. I read the full-size PNG, then re-cropped the ball region (x120-320, y140-290) at 3x with 1.6 gain and read that too, and additionally decoded the PNG in node to measure radial profiles, spike peaks, dot geometry and shadow extent at three independent luminance thresholds.

CORRECTION 1 - IT IS SEVEN LANCES, NOT EIGHT. Both s5 and s6 have exactly seven. Confirmed by eye at 3x (up-slightly-left, upper-right, long right horizontal, lower-right, small bottom, long left horizontal, long lower-left) and by radial peak detection, which returned 7 at thresholds 30, 55 and 90 and at a peak-normalised threshold. Anyone fixing this on the assumption of an eight-fold radial array will be editing the wrong loop.

CORRECTION 2 - THE ANGLES ARE THE DUPLICATE; THE LENGTHS ARE NOT. This is the load-bearing correction. Spike bearings (screen degrees, 0 = right, positive = downward): s5 = [0, 32, 114, 166, 193, 246, 328]; s6 = [0, 32, 115, 167, 193, 246, 328]. Identical to within 1 degree on all seven, across every threshold I tried - the angular skeleton is effectively locked between the two species. Ball radius 44.8 (s5) vs 44.0 (s6). BUT the lengths do vary: normalised to 22% of each image's own peak luminance, spike radii are s5 = [86.3, 70.0, 57.8, 90.3, 87.8, 51.5, 77.0] and s6 = [90.0, 74.3, 51.8, 83.3, 85.0, 56.8, 67.3] - differences of 3 to 10 px, up to 13%, and signed in both directions (+3.7, +4.3, -6.0, -7.0, -2.8, +5.3, -9.7), so this is real per-species jitter and not a thresholding artefact of teal-vs-white. The generator is already varying lance LENGTH per seed and is NOT varying lance ANGLE at all. The defect lives in the angle seed, not in a global 'make them different' knob.

CORRECTION 3 - NOT A PALETTE SWAP; TWO INDEPENDENT RENDERS THAT COLLIDED. The bright-pixel masks have IoU of only 0.80 at threshold 55 (0.84 at 60, 0.70 at 150) - a literal recolour of one bitmap would be 1.00. Beyond the length jitter, the two differ in lighting: s5 emits a broad teal ambient bloom that lifts the whole background field and washes out its own cast shadow (against a per-row local background reference my detector found 0 shadow pixels in s5 and 4,890 in s6), while s6 has a neutral warm vignette and a crisp black ellipse measuring 194 x 34 px, bbox [123,247] to [316,280], widest row y=263. s6 also carries a hotter specular, peak luminance 255 vs s5's 205, with 0.3% of the ball fully saturated. Diffing the two as colours would understate the bug: two separately rendered species landed on the same skeleton.

WHAT THE CLAIM GOT RIGHT AND SHOULD BE KEPT. The centre dot really is present in both, at the same place and the same size - s5's darkest in-ball pixel is at (222,196) rgb 56,144,146; s6's is at (220,197) rgb 124,123,120; measured dot diameters 10.4 px vs 11.0 px. It is not an s5-only feature and must not be 'restored' to s6, which already has it. One refinement: the dot sits about 11 px ABOVE the ball's geometric centre, not dead centre. The ground ellipses are also both centred on x=220 at comparable scale (s6 194 px wide; s5's edges read at x=130 and x=310, so about 180 px).

WRONG-ORGANISM CALL - SUSTAINED. A smooth glossy sphere with rigid, glass-straight radiating lances, a single dark sensor-like dot high on the face, and a cast-shadow ellipse reads as a naval contact mine, or secondarily a sea urchin or caltrop. There is no fungal cue anywhere on it: no cap, no stipe, no gills or pores, no bracket, no hyphae, no spore texture, no substrate attachment. The dot is a large part of why it reads as ordnance - it functions as an eye or a detonator. This is not a ceiling imposed by the generator: within this same batch, fungi-h2-s0 renders a convincing branching mycelial/coral canopy on stipes, fungi-h1-s8 a clump of pointed fruiting bodies, and fungi-h1-s4 a speckled puffball. So the family is not one chassis - s8 has 5 spikes at [34,149,233,283,314] with ball radius 89.5, s9 has 3 at [36,54,145], h2-s0 has 4 at [12,67,112,163] with ball radius 107.3, all genuinely distinct. The duplication is scoped precisely to the adjacent s5/s6 pair, which is where the fix belongs.

BAND. FAIL on two independent grounds, either of which is sufficient under this packet's stated criterion: (a) s6 is silhouette-indistinguishable from its immediate neighbour s5 - same seven bearings, same ball radius, same dot position and size, same ellipse - which is exactly the shared-body failure the batch header asks to be named; and (b) it does not read as a fungus at all.

rows.defect: Render defect, not just a read problem. A long dark-brown shallow arc spans almost the entire frame width, floating in empty space well ABOVE the yellow lobed body and never touching it — the substrate log has come unstuck from the organism it is supposed to support and is stranded in the sky. rows.verifyWhy:
Read the 440x440 PNG at full size, then a 3x nearest-neighbour crop of rows 120-340, then measured the pixels directly (System.Drawing row/column scans). Packet batch-012 line 25-27 gives this species reference row **NONE** (procedural — judge coherence against the batch), so there is no named must-read list to fail against; the only test is whether the render reads as a coherent organism. Generator is fungiJelly() in packages/art/src/proceduralfamilies.ts:116 — 'JELLY (tremelloid): a wet translucent lobed mass welded to a branch.'

WHAT IS ACTUALLY THERE. The tremelloid read is present and good. The yellow mass occupies x=169-305, y=208-306 (a 136x98 box, ~31% of frame width) and is built from ~7-10 overlapping soft lobes with visible fold seams, four distinct specular gloss caps (peak values 248,231,168) and dark lobe-to-lobe creases (down to 111,89,37). At 3x it unmistakably reads as glossy, wet, brain-folded witch's-butter — the correct organism, in the correct colour, with the gloss the code comment calls 'half the read'. The wood substrate is present too: a bark-brown bough (#2a1d15 core rendering at 51,36,26) arcing x=23-417, y=132-188 visible, with its rgba(0,0,0,0.38) underside stroke reaching y~199 (black on a near-black field, so effectively invisible). Nothing here reads as the wrong kingdom or the wrong family.

WHERE THE FAIL IS RIGHT. The mass is genuinely NOT attached. Minimum visible brown-bottom-to-yellow-top gap measured across x=150-320 is 21 px at x=207 (brown ends y=187, yellow begins y=208); at the frame centre (x=237) it is 27 px. Everything in that band is plain background (11-21 luminance). Code confirms the intent it misses: the branch is stroked along 0.30->0.44->0.34 of S while the mass is centred at cy = S*0.56 with lobe radii of only 0.055-0.11 S, so the two shapes cannot overlap by construction. A mass described as 'welded' and 'gripping' floats clear of its branch. That is a real composition defect and worth fixing.

WHERE THE FAIL IS WRONG — three corrections the fix must not be made against.
1. 'Stranded in empty space WELL ABOVE' overstates it by an order of magnitude. The gap is 21-27 px in a 440 px frame — 5-6% of frame height, about a fifth of the body's own height. It is a hairline void, not a stranded element in a different part of the canvas. The branch sits directly over the mass, correctly centred on it; the arc even dips toward the mass at centre. The fix is to close ~25 px, not to relocate anything.
2. 'Spanning the full frame width' is factually true (x=23-417, 89% of frame) but is not a defect and should not be 'fixed'. A branch crossing the frame edge-to-edge is the intended composition for a tremelloid and matches fungiTooth's bough in the same file. Do not shorten it.
3. 'The body itself has no ground shadow and floats too' — the absence is real (fungiJelly is the one fungal family in this file that never calls ground(); I confirmed there is no dark ellipse anywhere below y=306, only a smooth warm ambient glow rising from 9,9,11 to 15,13,10), but the prescription is WRONG. A jelly fungus hanging off a bough is not standing on soil; adding ground() at S*0.84 would put a floor shadow under an epiphyte and make the render less correct, not more. What is missing is CONTACT shading against the branch, not a ground shadow.

CORRECT FIX. Raise the mass (cy from S*0.56 to roughly S*0.47-0.50) and/or drop the branch, so the upper lobes overlap the bough by ~15-20 px; draw the topmost one or two lobes before the branch stroke so the bark edge clips over them and they read as gripping; then add a small dark occlusion smear on the branch underside where the lobes meet it, in place of a ground ellipse.

BAND. Both identity elements — glossy lobed jelly mass and wood substrate — are present, large and readable; nothing defining is absent and it does not read as another organism. A 21 px attachment gap is a positional polish, not a broken render. POLISH, FAIL not upheld.

WHAT I ACTUALLY SAW. I read the PNG at native exposure, then re-decoded it and re-rendered four boosted/upscaled crops (whole frame, 3x centre, 4x base band y230-340, 4x top band y120-210) plus a pixel measurement pass. Subject bbox on the 440x440 canvas is x104-328, y140-276 — 51% of the width but only 31% of the height, a squat horizontal pair. It is two overlapping circles: left centre ~x170 r~68, right centre ~x272 r~56, overlapping ~35px, both centres at nearly the same height (~y208). Each carries a soft diffuse light-to-dark gradient and a scatter of roughly 45-55 flat dark circular dots (radius 2-8px). There is a detached soft elliptical ground shadow centred ~y285. That is the entire asset.

THE FAIL STANDS. No fungal must-read is present at any scale. There is no cap (no pileus dome distinct from anything below it, no margin, no incurved edge, no umbo). There is no stipe: I zoomed the base band 4x at 3.2x gain and the left sphere's lower contour is a clean unbroken circular arc that terminates at y=276 and touches nothing — no stalk, no volva, no basal mycelium, no substrate attachment. The spheres float clear of the shadow ellipse. There is no hymenium cue: no gills, no radial lines, no pore field, no warts, no annulus, no veil remnant. The top band at 4x is featureless smooth curvature. It reads as two boulders / a contact-binary asteroid, exactly as claimed.

I DELIBERATELY TRIED THE CHARITABLE READING AND IT FAILS. A pair of spheres could legitimately be a puffball cluster (Lycoperdon/Bovista are genuinely stipeless spheres), which would rescue the 'no cap, no stipe' objection. It does not survive inspection: puffballs need a warty/spiny/granular or areolate skin, an apical ostiole, and a tapered sterile base sunk into the substrate. Here the skin is perfectly smooth, the dots are RECESSED (flat dark fill, no highlight rim, no cast shadow) so they read as craters not warts, the apex is completely blank, and there is no base and no substrate contact.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM (fix against these, not the original wording):
1. 'Matte' is WRONG and this matters most. The render is not matte — the highest-contrast element in the entire image is a hard bright specular rim arc, one per sphere. Peak rim luminance is L=146 (at x230,y169) sitting on a body whose core samples are RGB(43,45,59) on the left sphere and RGB(51,53,70) on the right, i.e. L~45-60. The rim is a 2-3px near-white hard-edged crescent running roughly 10 to 12 o'clock on the left sphere (x123-183, y140-165) and 12 o'clock down the right flank to about 4 o'clock on the right sphere (x230 to x328, y150-227). That glossy hard edge-light is a large part of what makes this read mineral/ceramic rather than organic. Killing or softening it is a required part of any fix.
2. 'Slate' understates how dark this is. At true exposure the body is near-black blue-violet; nothing but the two rim arcs clears L=70. Under-exposure is an independent defect the original judge did not flag — even if the morphology were corrected, the asset would still barely read on a dark card.
3. 'Desaturated' relative to h1-s4 is DIRECTIONALLY WRONG. I rendered fungi-h1-s4 for comparison: it is a single PALE near-white blue sphere, noticeably brighter than s9. s9 is darker and slightly more violet — darkened and hue-shifted, not desaturated. The rest of that sentence is correct: it is unmistakably the same primitive (sphere + scattered recessed pits + rim arc) instanced twice at two radii.
4. The pit scatter has a second flaw the claim did not name: the dots are distributed only across the flat front face of each sphere and do not wrap the curvature into the terminator, so they read as decals on a disc and actively flatten the form.
5. Not a generator-wide limitation. Sibling fungi-h1-s8 in the same batch renders a legible upright coral-fungus spine cluster, so this family can produce non-spherical fungal morphology. s9 is this species falling back to a bare sphere primitive, not a family ceiling.

FIX DIRECTION IMPLIED: give it a vertical axis and a ground contact. A cap/stipe silhouette or, if the spherical body plan is to be kept, commit to a puffball — warty or granular skin with raised warts that cast their own micro-shadows, an apical pore at the crown, a tapered sterile base merging into substrate/mycelium, and remove the hard specular rim in favour of a soft organic terminator. Also raise overall value: the body must clear the background without a boosted exposure.

CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM. 1) "Thin UNFILLED outline ellipse" is wrong — there is a filled interior with a gradient; it only reads as empty because the fill peaks around 40% of the membrane's luminance and the interior sits at rgb(100,50,43) against a rgb(6,9,15) ground, so at native size the bright stroke dominates and the mass disappears. The fix is to raise interior value and lower stroke contrast, NOT to "add a fill" — the fill exists. 2) "Radial hairs" is wrong — the ribs are not radial and are not hairs. They are all parallel and vertical regardless of where they sit on the ellipse, so they are not normal to the membrane, they never break the silhouette, and their length is set purely by where the chord meets the outline. That geometry is exactly why the thing reads as hatch marks / scale ticks on a gauge. Cilia on a ciliate must leave the body outline, follow the membrane normal, and vary in length and phase. 3) "One dotted horizontal axis line" is correct and is the single most damaging element: a perfectly straight pole-to-pole bar with a dot at each end and one in the middle is the visual grammar of a dimension line or an axle, and it is what pushes the read from "cell" to "CAD diagram".

ON "no volume or shading" — half right. There IS shading: the radial gradient plus the specular arc. But the gradient is perfectly symmetric top-to-bottom (y=169 reads 91, y=273 reads 88 on the same column), so it carries no light direction; there is no terminator, no bounce/rim on the lower edge, and no cytoplasm texture or organelle. The lone arc highlight is also the wrong hue — a grey-white that does not belong to the orange palette. So the form is lit like a glow, not like a body.

Siblings show what the family can do: microbe-h1-s10 is a cluster of flagellates with real modelled volume and long trailing flagella; microbe-h1-s12 is a coccus with a proper specular, terminator and settled interior. Against those, s11 is the outlier — it is the only member that resolves to a geometric primitive with tick marks. No shared-chassis problem here; the problem is the opposite, s11 does not belong to the same rendering standard.

WHY FAIL AND NOT POLISH. The identity is not readable: nothing in the image says single-celled organism. Perfect ellipse, perfect bilateral AND vertical mirror symmetry, uniform ticks, ruler bar with end caps — a viewer names this a stadium plan, a turbine hub or a measurement gauge before they name it a microbe. The defining must-read for the ciliate archetype (cilia that project past the membrane) is absent, not merely small or misplaced: I checked the rows just outside the silhouette (y=120, y=290, and the columns beyond x=69/370) and they are pure background, so nothing protrudes anywhere. This needs a re-draw of the ciliary fringe and removal of the axial bar, not a polish pass.

Both endpoint angles (0.3 and PI-0.3) have equal sine, so filling the arc closes it with a straight HORIZONTAL chord. The result is a half-disc, flat side up - a fluid line, not a cup. I measured all four: widths 150 / 146 / 152 / 154 px -- effectively identical -- and heights 144 / 136 / 158 / 172, i.e. aspect 0.960 / 0.932 / 1.039 / 1.117. The ONLY parameters that move across the four instances are vertical stretch and hue. Same centre, same width, same rim stroke, same upper-left specular, same speck field, same horizontal fill line. So 'fourth copy of the glass-marble chassis' is literally correct, and the confirmed generator behaviour is: fixed-width ellipse, height jittered ~+/-13%, hue rotated. Worse than the judge stated -- h1-s8 is not merely the nearest sibling in silhouette, it is also the SAME GREEN, so h2-s0 and h1-s8 differ only by an 8% aspect change and nothing else legible.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE CLAIM, neither of which rescues it. (1) 'Same speck-bubbles' is loose: h1-s8 carries three specks plus a small comma/streak mark BELOW its fill line, whereas h2-s0 has five specks and all five sit ABOVE the line, with nothing in the settled region. (2) 'Stretched into a slight oval' understates it slightly -- the ellipse is 12% taller than wide (h1-s8 is 4%), which is the largest deviation of the four, but it is still the only axis of variation, so the point stands.

WHY THIS IS FAIL AND NOT POLISH. There is no reference row, so no named must-read is absent; the failure is the other kind the brief calls out -- the asset reads as the wrong object. Set against its own batch-mates, which are genuinely specific organisms (h1-s19 magenta spirochetes with tapering terminal flagella, h1-s3 a teal tardigrade with segmented cuticle, stubby legs and eye spots, h1-s5 a heliozoan with radiating axopods, h1-s6 purple filaments with terminal bulbs, h2-s11 discrete bacilli rods, h2-s10 a swarm cloud), this marble carries zero organism vocabulary: no nucleus, no organelles, no membrane texture, no granularity, no locomotion structure, no polarity, no size cue. Nothing in the image names a living thing. Fix direction: kill the horizontal meniscus outright (it is the single strongest anti-life signal), replace the hard specular disc with a soft off-axis sheen, give the rim a variable-width lipid-bilayer read with a slight lobed/amoeboid deviation from the perfect ellipse, and add at least one interior structure with actual form -- a shaded nucleus with a nucleolus, contractile vacuoles with rims, or chloroplast bands -- plus a per-seed appendage (cilia band, one or two flagella, or pseudopods) so the four marbles stop being one object in four hues.

rows.verifyWhy:
Verdict upheld, but THREE of the four stated causes are factually wrong and must not be used as the fix brief.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY IN THE FRAME (440x440, background 5,6,12): a soft-edged green haze occupying the middle of the canvas, carrying ~250 small pale-mint rod strokes, ~10 translucent grey discs, and ~8 long curved filaments streaming off the right side.

CORRECTION 1 -- "runs off all four edges / clipped on every side" is FALSE, measured. I scanned every border pixel: on rows 0, 3, 10, h-11, h-4, h-1 and cols 0, 3, 10, w-11, w-4, w-1 the count of pixels above a background threshold is ZERO on every one, and the peak border value is 31/765 (i.e. plain vignette, not content). The content bounding box is x 25..417, y 73..365 -- margins of 25px left, 23px right, 73px top, 75px bottom. The mass is fully contained; the bottom crop shows a distinctly hard, almost horizontal lower silhouette edge with two lobes hanging below it, and the left crop shows a lobed, cauliflower-like colony margin. There IS a boundary; it is soft and unmembraned, not absent.

CORRECTION 2 -- "the only concrete forms are tick-marks and grey circles" misses the flagella. There are roughly eight long, smoothly curved, tapering filaments sweeping off the right flank between y~110 and y~350, terminating around x=416. They are the clearest drawn forms in the picture and they establish a left-to-right axis. Any fix brief that omits them will delete the one good element.

CORRECTION 3 -- "tick-marks" undersells them. At 3x magnification they are unambiguous bacilli: capsule-ended rods ~10-14px long, many bent into V/chevron pairs in a convincing corynebacterial 'chinese-letter' arrangement. The microbe identity reads. Nobody would call this smoke or a nebula once they look at the rods.

WHERE THE JUDGE IS RIGHT. (a) The grey discs really do read as lens dirt. I scanned one at (266,120): interior is a near-uniform 60,80,75 varying by ~5 levels across its whole 16px width, with only a 1-2px top rim at 72,87,85. They are flat neutral-grey semi-transparent fills with no volume, no rim light, no internal structure, and no hue relationship to the green -- exactly the signature of dust on a sensor. (b) There is no scale cue and no subject.

WHY IT STILL FAILS -- and the real reason. Judged against its own batch, which the packet explicitly instructs (reference row is NONE). Siblings s1, s11, s14 and s5 all render the same family as a SMALL NUMBER OF DISCRETE, VOLUMETRICALLY SHADED ORGANISMS on dark ground: s11 is eight 100px+ bacilli with a clear top-left key light and a shadow side; s1 and s14 are streptococcus chains of fully modelled spheres; s5 is a lit tardigrade. Every one of them has a protagonist and a lighting model. s10 has neither. Its rods are flat unlit fills at a tenth the sibling scale, its discs are flat fills, and its body is an unlit fog -- so the card depicts a substrate, a petri-dish field or biofilm mat, rather than a creature. That is a whole-idiom mismatch, not a cleanup: the fix is to re-author it as a few large, painterly, lit cells (keep the flagella, keep the chevron rod pairs as the identity, drop or re-light the grey discs), not to crop, re-frame, or add a membrane.

rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD, with three factual corrections to the stated cause. WHAT I SAW at full size and again at 6x nearest-neighbour zoom on the upper-right quadrant: a 440x440 canvas, near-black navy field, and one centred disc of radius 132px (30% of canvas). The disc is a radial gradient, brightest at the exact centre and falling off monotonically to near-black at the margin. Over it sit exactly four circles and a fan of straight radial spokes. Nothing else is on the canvas. CORRECTION 1 - the spoke count is 17, not 16. I sampled 2000 points around a circle at r=115 (between the outermost interior ring and the rim) and counted 17 threshold crossings at 0, 21.1, 42.2, 63.6, 85.0, 106.1, 127.5, 148.6, 169.6, 190.9, 211.8, 233.0, 253.9, 274.9, 296.2, 317.2, 338.4 degrees - a perfectly even 21.2-degree pitch with zero jitter. CORRECTION 2 - s13 and s19 are NOT geometrically identical. The same sweep on microbe-h2-s19 returns 15 spokes at a 24.0-degree pitch. Everything else does match exactly (same rim radius, same three interior rings, same hub radius, same gradient, differing only in hue: s13 is cold blue-grey, s19 is violet). So the pair is not literally the same file; it is the same construction with two spokes' difference and a hue swap, which is indistinguishable to a player and still a real repetition defect - the judge's conclusion survives, the word 'identical' does not. CORRECTION 3 - the stroke is 1.6px, not 1px, and the outer rim is drawn TWICE at full alpha while the spokes and interior rings are at ~0.5 alpha. That is why the rim is the loudest mark on the canvas (I measured luminance-sum 637 at the rim versus ~349 peak on an interior ring), and it is the single biggest driver of the bicycle-wheel read: the brightest thing in the picture is a geometrically perfect circle. THE CORE OF THE CLAIM IS CONFIRMED AND IS WORSE THAN STATED. I sampled a radial luminance profile along a ray at 10.5 degrees, deliberately threaded between two spokes, from r=0 to r=160. It reads 386 at centre and decays by 1-3 units per pixel, monotonically, all the way out - interrupted only by three narrow ring spikes at r=33, r=65 and r=98, and the rim at r=131. Between those spikes there is not one pixel of high-frequency variation. That is proof, not impression: there are zero areolae, zero punctae, zero costae shading, zero silica grain, no central annulus, no rimoportulae, no cingulum, no cell contents (no plastids, no nucleus, no cytoplasm) anywhere inside the valve. A centric diatom's entire visual identity is the hexagonal/radial pore array in the silica; this asset draws the scaffolding those pores would sit on and then leaves every sector empty. On volume: the judge said 'no volume', which is right in effect but slightly wrong in description - there IS a radial gradient, but it is centre-bright and perfectly axisymmetric with no directional light and no offset specular, so it reads as a backlit radar screen or a lens flare, not as a glass frustule with thickness. Note the spokes stop short at r=26 (0.06 of canvas) and just end in mid-air around a bare gradient blob, leaving 17 raw stub-ends at the hub - there is no central area to terminate into. ROOT CAUSE, for whoever fixes this: packages/art/src/speciesoverrides.ts, function microbeDiatom (~line 280). The function forks on 'const radial = r() < 0.5'. The PENNATE branch was rebuilt in Wave 20 and now has a raphe, three nodules, striae that fan and stop at the valve curve, and a white lens highlight along the upper face. The RADIAL branch below it was never touched - it is still the original wireframe, and it even contains a copy-paste bug: 'c.beginPath(); c.arc(...); c.stroke();' for the outer circle appears twice in a row, which is exactly the double-bright rim I measured. s13 and s19 both landed on the radial branch. The fix is to give the radial branch the same treatment the pennate branch already got. BATCH CONTEXT: the packet has no reference row for this species and asks for coherence against its 13 batch-mates. I looked at three - s12 is a soft volumetric biofilm colony with hundreds of bacilli and flagella, s14 is a rendered pink streptococcus chain with per-coccus specular highlights, s17 is a fully shaded tardigrade with segmented cuticle, eight clawed legs and a cast ground shadow. So the batch is NOT one chassis (that specific packet worry does not apply here). But it means s13 sits beside genuinely painted organisms as the only flat vector diagram in the set, which also puts it in direct conflict with the HD engine law that forbids flat primitives. FAIL is the correct band.

rows.verifyWhy:
UPHELD, but three parts of the stated cause are wrong and one real defect was missed. WHAT I SAW (440x440, centre 220,220): a violet radially-spoked, concentrically-ringed disc on the dark vignette field, nothing else in frame -- no flagella, no cilia, no fringe, no organelles, no nucleus, no debris.

MEASURED (PNG decoded and radially profiled, not eyeballed):
- Ring radii are IDENTICAL to s13. Luminance peaks along +x land at r=33/65/99/131 in s19 and r=32/65/99/131 in s13; the outer edge measures 132.0-133.5 px at all eight compass angles in BOTH files. So 'same radius, same three rings' is exactly correct and is the strongest part of the claim -- three inner annuli plus the rim, same construction, same size.
- 'Same sixteen spokes' is WRONG on both counts. Angular peak detection at r=50/80/115 gives s19 = 15 costae at 24.0 deg pitch (peaks 23.8, 47.8, 72.6 ... 335.3) and s13 = 17 costae at 21.2 deg pitch (20.6, 42.3, 63.8 ... 338.4). Neither is 16 and they are not the same. So it is not literally a pure hue swap -- it is hue plus a +/-1 spoke setting, a difference nobody can perceive, which arguably makes the redundancy point worse rather than rescuing it. Do not tell the fixer 'the spoke count is shared'; it is not, and the generator clearly already varies it.
- 'Flat disc' is imprecise. The interior is a strong radial vignette: mean ring luminance 116 at centre, 107 at r=20, 97 at r=40, 67 at r=80, 34 at r=120, 23 at r=128, then a single bright stroke at r=132 (154) and straight to background (13) at r=136. So the body FADES OUT into the backdrop before its own rim, and the rim is one hairline. That is why it reads as an empty wire wheel or a tilted dish rather than a filled cell -- not because the fill is flat, but because the fill is dark exactly where the silhouette needs to be legible. There is no glow, no soft membrane edge, no rim thickness; the organism ends in one anti-aliased pixel.
- 'Wagon wheel rather than a cell' is the part I want to correct in spirit even though the band stands. The SCHEMA is legitimate biology: a radially costate, concentrically annulate disc is precisely a centric diatom valve (Arachnoidiscus, literally nicknamed 'wheel of glass'; Actinoptychus). This is not the wrong organism. What is absent is every rendering cue that would sell a silica frustule -- areolae/punctae (the pore field), any variation in costa weight from hub to margin, a thickened or beaded marginal ring, a defined hyaline central area, and any specular value break. The fix is 'render the valve', NOT 'redesign the organism'. A fixer told to abandon the wheel would throw away the one correct thing here.

DEFECT THE JUDGE MISSED: at 4x on the centre, the costae have ragged, uneven inner terminations. They stop at scattered radii around the r=33 annulus -- several as short stubs ending well outside it, several crossing inside it -- so the hub is a scruffy corona of unfinished line ends instead of a central area. At the margin at least one costa stops roughly 15 px short of the outer arc. This is unfinished geometry, visible and fixable independently of the texture problem.

BATCH COHERENCE (the packet has no reference row and directs judging against the batch): the family is NOT one chassis -- s12 and s16 are granular colony clouds with punctate granules and trailing flagella, s4 is a cluster of rendered teardrop flagellates with sheen and red nuclei, s18 is a teal ciliate with a full cilia fringe, membrane and internal vacuoles. Against those, s19 is the only member drawn in bare uniform-width hairline vector over a gradient, with zero surface texture at any radius. It is the rendering outlier of the batch and violates the HD engine law's no-flat-primitives rule, and its only true twin is s13. FAIL stands on rendering fidelity and on carrying no information s13 does not.

rows.readsAs: a green marble, or a jar half full of liquid
rows.defect: There is no organism here at all. rows.verifyWhy: UPHELD, but two-thirds of the stated causes are wrong and the fix list must be rewritten. What is actually on canvas (440x440, verified by pixel scan and by 5x nearest-neighbour + gamma-0.42 crops): a mathematically perfect circle, bbox 145,147-294,292 = 150x146 px, centre ~(220,220), r~75. I scanned row extents at y=100..320: rows 150/180/215/240/260/280/290 give a clean circular chord progression and rows 100-130 and 300-320 are empty. There is ZERO geometry outside the circle - no cilia, no flagellum, no pseudopod, no pilus, no stalk, not one pixel. That is the real defect and it is fatal: the silhouette carries no organism information at all. CORRECTION 1 - 'no membrane' is false. There IS a continuous membrane/wall stroke: a ~2px pale grey-green rim running the full circumference, brightest on the upper-left arc and still legible at the bottom. It is thin and generic but it is present, so 'add a membrane' is not the fix. CORRECTION 2 - 'flat-shaded' is false and this matters. The body carries a proper radial diffuse gradient with the light from the upper left: a warm yellow-green core around (195,190) falling off to dark olive at the lower-right limb, plus limb darkening at the edges. It is competently shaded - and that is exactly WHY it reads as a marble or a distant planet rather than as a cell. Removing the sphere-volume lighting in favour of translucent cytoplasm is part of the fix; adding shading is not. CORRECTION 3 - 'three tiny dots' undercounts; there are FIVE. Separately from the specular blob (a hard-edged near-white disc r~9px centred about (194,190)), five flat uniform pale-green discs of r~4px are scattered with no pattern down the middle-right of the body, at source coords approx (212,204), (229,215), (248,232), (204,240) and (230,255). They read as flat stickers, not organelles - no rim, no nucleolus, no shadow, no depth cue, and they do not scale or dim as they cross into the darker lower zone. CORRECTION 4 - the horizontal chord is correctly identified and is worse than described. It is a dead-straight, perfectly horizontal line at y~245 (about 28% up from the bottom of the circle). The region below it is a SINGLE FLAT GREEN with literally no gradient - it does not participate in the sphere's lighting at all, it is not darkened at the left or right limb, and it terminates hard against the rim stroke on both sides. Gamma-boosting the shadows to 0.42 confirms there is nothing hidden in it. The result is unmistakably a meniscus - a half-filled jar or a lava-lamp fluid line. One of the five dots floats below the line inside the flat zone, which reinforces the 'sediment in liquid' read. Whatever this element is meant to be (a vacuole? a basal body? a pigment cup?), a horizontal chord is the one shape it must never be: it must curve, follow the body's lighting, or be replaced. CORRECTION 5 - there is no interior structure of any kind besides the five dots and the fill line. Gamma boost shows no nucleus, no cytoplasmic granulation, no vacuole outlines, no cell-wall texture. BATCH CONTEXT (the packet gives no reference row: 'procedural or unlisted - judge coherence, and judge it against the others in this batch'). Judged against its own batch this is far below the bar. microbe-h2-s5 is a legible tardigrade - segmented cuticle ribs, eight clawed stub legs, a distinct head lobe with two eye spots, contact shadow. microbe-h2-s7 is a legible flagellate - two tapered lobes, two long curling flagella, two red eyespots. s6 is not the same class of drawing; it would be indistinguishable from a decorative planet or bauble if dropped into any other set. FAIL stands on the absent identity, not on absent shading.

rows.readsAs: two golden flagellated protozoa
